fig.caption: More open surface, more water escaping as vapour — the plate empties much faster than the tumbler.
fig.alt: A wide plate and a tall tumbler with vapour bubbles rising faster from the plate

check.q: In the puddle investigation, which one thing was changed?
check.why: Only the container's width was changed, while the volume of water, place and time were kept the same for a fair test.

sections.md:
Imagine you want to know whether seeds sprout better with water or without. You put moong seeds with water in a steel bowl on a sunny window and dry seeds in a plastic box inside a cupboard. The wet ones sprout. Did water make the difference — or the sunlight, or the type of container, or the warmth?

That test was **unfair**, because too many things changed at once.

In a **fair test**, you change **only one thing** and keep everything else the same:

| Keep the same | Change only this | Measure this |
|---|---|---|
| type and number of seeds, container, place, temperature | water / no water | how many seeds sprout in 3 days |

The thing you change is sometimes called the **variable**. Using **more than one** seed (say 20 in each bowl) and repeating the test makes the result more reliable — one seed could be a dud.

**Recording results** carefully in a notebook, with dates and numbers, is part of good science. A table of results can then be turned into a bar graph (as you learn in maths!).

check.q: To test whether sunlight affects how fast ice melts, what should you keep the same?
options: Only the colour of the plate
The size of the ice cube, the plate and the starting temperature
check.why: In a fair test only sunlight should change, so the ice size, container and starting conditions must be kept the same.

sections.h: Asking good questions and staying curious
sections.md:
Some questions are easier to test than others.

- 'Why is the sky so pretty?' — hard to test; 'pretty' is an opinion.
- 'Does the sky look a different colour at sunset than at noon?' — you can observe and record!

Good scientific questions are **specific** and can be answered by **observation or experiment**.

**Habits of a young scientist:**

- **Observe closely** — use all your senses safely (never taste unknown things!).
- **Keep a science diary** — draw, measure, note the date.
- **Ask 'why?' and 'what if?'** — what if I use salt water? What if it is dark?
- **Be honest** about results, even if they surprise you.
- **Work together** — scientists share ideas and check each other's work.
- **Be safe** — take an adult's help with heat, sharp tools or electricity.

Curiosity is also about respecting nature: observe ants without destroying their nest, look at flowers without plucking them all.

> **Did you know?** C. V. Raman wondered why the Mediterranean Sea looked so blue during a ship voyage in 1921. His curiosity led to the discovery of the *Raman effect* in 1928 and the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics. India celebrates **National Science Day** on 28 February, the date the discovery was announced.

check.q: Which question is easiest to test scientifically?
options: Do plants kept in the dark grow taller or shorter than plants in light?
check.why: Plant height in light versus dark can be measured in a fair test, while the other questions depend on opinion.

sections.h: Thinking like a scientist about everyday claims
sections.md:
Science is not only for laboratories — it helps you decide what to believe. Every day you hear claims: a forwarded message says drinking hot water cures every illness; an advertisement says a toothpaste makes teeth '10 times stronger'; a friend says eclipses are dangerous to look at.

A scientific thinker asks:

- **What is the evidence?** Has anyone tested it fairly, with many people or samples?
- **Who is making the claim, and why?** Is someone trying to sell something?
- **Can I test it, or check a trusted source?** Your teacher, textbooks, and official bodies such as health departments are good places to check.
- **Does it make sense with what I already know?**

Some claims turn out true: looking straight at the Sun during an eclipse really *can* hurt your eyes, so we use proper eclipse glasses or a pinhole projector. Others have no evidence.

**Science is also humble.** Scientists change their ideas when new evidence appears. People once believed the Sun went round the Earth; careful observations showed the opposite. Being willing to say 'I was wrong' is a scientific strength, not a weakness.

**Science as a career.** Curiosity can grow into a job: doctors, farmers testing new seeds, weather scientists at the India Meteorological Department, engineers at ISRO, forest officers studying tigers, chefs perfecting recipes — all use observation and testing every day.

check.q: A message claims a drink makes you taller in a week. What is the most scientific first response?
options: Ask what evidence supports it and check a trusted source
check.why: Scientific thinking asks for evidence and checks reliable sources before accepting a claim.

check.q: Which Indian scientist explained that the Earth rotates on its axis?
check.why: Aryabhata, born in 476 CE, proposed that the Earth spins on its axis, explaining the apparent daily motion of the stars.

story.title: The Mystery of the Shy Leaves

parts.md: Ananya spent her summer holidays at her grandmother's house in a village near Mysuru. Behind the cowshed grew a low plant with tiny feathery leaves. One morning, while chasing a butterfly, Ananya brushed the plant with her hand — and the leaves folded up at once, as if shy! She gasped and touched another branch. It folded too. 'Ajji, is this plant alive like us?' she called. Ajji smiled. 'We call it *naachike gida* — the shy plant. In books they call it *touch-me-not*, or *Mimosa pudica*.'

Ananya decided to be a scientist. She **observed**: the leaves folded when touched and opened again after some minutes. She **asked**: how long do they take to open? Do they fold if I blow on them? Her **guess** was that a strong breeze would also make them fold. She tested it: a gentle blow — nothing; a sharp puff — some leaflets closed. She touched different branches and timed the reopening with Ajji's wall clock: about 10 to 15 minutes each time. She wrote it all in a notebook.

Back in school, she showed her notebook to her science teacher, who was delighted. 'You followed the scientific method!' he said, and explained that the plant moves water out of special cells at the base of its leaflets, making them droop — and slowly refills them later. Nobody had given Ananya the answer first; she had found her own evidence. That evening she wrote a new question on the next page: *Do the leaves also fold at night, when nobody touches them?* The adventure continued.

summary: Science is a way of understanding the world through questions, observation and evidence.
Curiosity — asking 'why?' and 'what if?' — drives science.
Science is everywhere: kitchen, garden, sky, playground and our bodies.
Technology like phones, vaccines and satellites grows out of science.
Scientific method: observe, question, hypothesise, experiment, analyse, conclude, share.
A hypothesis is a testable guess.
A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same.
Repeating tests and using many samples makes results reliable.
Unexpected results are useful — they lead to new ideas.
Good questions are specific and testable.
Check everyday claims by asking for evidence and trusted sources.
Be honest, careful and safe; respect living things.
C. V. Raman's discovery is celebrated on National Science Day, 28 February.
Indian contributors to science include Aryabhata, Sushruta, J. C. Bose and Janaki Ammal.

glossary.d: Noticing and recording something using the senses or instruments.
A testable guess that explains an observation.
A planned test of a hypothesis.
A test where only one factor is changed.
What the evidence shows about the hypothesis.
Water changing into vapour and mixing with the air.

sections.h: A walk that changes how you see
Grouping plants by height and stem
sections.md:
Walk up to any plant and the first thing you notice is its size. Scientists use size together with the nature of the stem to group plants into three familiar types.

| Type | Height | Stem | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Herbs** | Short, usually under 1 m | Green, soft, tender | Tulsi, wheat, mint, grass, coriander |
| **Shrubs** | Medium, 1–3 m | Hard, woody, many branches near the base | Rose, hibiscus (gudhal), lemon, henna |
| **Trees** | Tall | Thick, hard, woody trunk; branches higher up | Mango, neem, banyan, peepal, coconut |

Notice the trick for shrubs versus trees: a shrub branches **close to the ground**, so it looks bushy; a tree has a single strong **trunk** before branching.

Some plants have stems too weak to stand upright:

- **Climbers** use support to climb upward — money plant, pea, grapevine, bottle gourd on a trellis. Many have thin curly **tendrils** that wrap around a stick.
- **Creepers** spread along the ground — pumpkin, watermelon, sweet potato.

Why would a plant climb? Sunlight! A climber reaches light high up without spending energy building a thick trunk.

check.q: A rose plant is about 1.5 m tall and has hard stems branching close to the soil. It is a:

sections.md:
Pick a leaf of peepal and hold it up to the sunlight. You will see a network of fine lines — the **veins**. They carry water into the leaf and food out of it, like tiny pipes. The pattern of veins is called **venation**.

There are two main patterns:

1. **Reticulate venation** — veins form a **net** on both sides of a thick central vein (the midrib). Seen in peepal, mango, hibiscus, tulsi, rose.
2. **Parallel venation** — veins run **side by side** along the length of the leaf. Seen in grass, wheat, maize, banana, bamboo, sugarcane.

A simple activity: place a thin paper over a leaf and rub a crayon sideways over it. The venation appears like magic — a **leaf rubbing**.

Parts of a leaf worth knowing: the flat green part is the **lamina** (leaf blade), the stalk joining it to the stem is the **petiole**, and the central thick vein is the **midrib**.

check.q: Which leaf shows parallel venation?
check.why: Banana, like grass and maize, has veins running side by side along the leaf.

sections.md:
Now dig gently around a small mustard or bean plant, and around a tuft of grass or a wheat plant (with permission, and replant afterwards!). Wash off the soil and compare.

- **Taproot**: one thick main root growing straight down, with thinner **lateral roots** branching from it. Seen in mustard, bean, carrot, radish, mango, hibiscus.
- **Fibrous roots**: a bunch of thin roots of about equal size that grow out from the base of the stem — no single main root. Seen in grass, wheat, maize, rice, onion.

Here is the exciting pattern scientists noticed: **plants with reticulate venation usually have taproots, and plants with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots.** By looking at the leaf, you can often predict the root without digging!

| Leaf venation | Root type | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Reticulate | Taproot | Mustard, tulsi, hibiscus, mango |
| Parallel | Fibrous | Grass, wheat, maize, banana |

Roots do two big jobs: they **anchor** the plant firmly in soil, and they **absorb water and minerals**. Some roots like carrot and radish also **store food**.

> **Did you know?** A single rye plant grown in a lab was found to have roots totalling hundreds of kilometres when all the fine root hairs were measured end to end.

keyTerms: Taproot — one main root with side branches
Fibrous roots — many similar thin roots from the stem base
Lateral roots — side branches of a taproot

check.q: A plant has leaves with parallel venation. Its roots are most likely:
check.why: Parallel venation usually goes together with a fibrous root system, as in grass and wheat.

sections.md:
There is one more clue hidden inside plants — in their **seeds**. Soak a few chana (gram) or rajma seeds and a few maize or wheat grains in water overnight.

Next morning, gently peel the chana seed. It splits easily into **two equal halves**. Each half is a **cotyledon** (seed leaf) — a store of food for the baby plant. Now try the maize grain: it does **not** split into two; it has only **one** cotyledon.

- Plants whose seeds have **two cotyledons** are called **dicotyledons** (dicots): chana, rajma, moong, pea, mustard, mango, neem.
- Plants whose seeds have **one cotyledon** are called **monocotyledons** (monocots): maize, wheat, rice, barley, grass, banana, onion.

Now put all our clues together. A remarkable pattern appears:

| Feature | Dicots | Monocots |
|---|---|---|
| Cotyledons in seed | Two | One |
| Leaf venation | Reticulate | Parallel |
| Roots | Taproot | Fibrous |
| Examples | Chana, mustard, mango | Wheat, maize, rice |

So if you know one feature, you can often predict the others! This is the power of careful grouping — patterns let scientists make predictions. (Nature has exceptions, so always check by observing.)

**Watch it grow:** keep the soaked seeds on wet cotton for a few days. You will see the **radicle** (baby root) poke out first, then the shoot. In chana, the two cotyledons may rise with the shoot and shrink as their food is used up.

keyTerms: Cotyledon — seed leaf that stores food
Dicot — two cotyledons
Monocot — one cotyledon
Radicle — the first, baby root

check.q: A seed has two cotyledons. Its plant most likely has:
check.why: Dicots, with two cotyledons, usually have net-like (reticulate) venation and a taproot.

sections.h: Animals: grouping by what we observe
sections.md:
Animals are even more varied than plants. We can group them using simple observable features:

- **How they move**: walk (cow, dog), fly (sparrow, bat), swim (fish), crawl (snail, earthworm), hop (frog), slither (snake).
- **Where they live**: land, water, both, trees, underground.
- **What they eat**: plants only (**herbivores** — cow, deer, rabbit), animals only (**carnivores** — tiger, lion), both (**omnivores** — crow, bear, humans).
- **Body covering**: hair/fur, feathers, scales, shell.

There is no single "correct" grouping — it depends on the feature you choose. A bat and a sparrow both fly, but a bat has fur and feeds its young on milk, so scientists group it with mammals, not birds. Grouping is a tool for thinking clearly.

Try it: make a table with columns *Animal, Moves by, Eats, Body covering, Lives in* and fill it for ten animals from your neighbourhood. You'll quickly see patterns — and exceptions.

head: Animal
Moves by
Eats
Covering
Lives
fig.caption: One way to group animals by observable features.

check.q: A crow eats grains, fruit, insects and scraps. It is a:
check.why: An animal that eats both plant and animal food is an omnivore.

sections.md:
The place where a plant or animal naturally lives and finds food, water, shelter and mates is its **habitat**. Habitats can be **terrestrial** (on land — forests, grasslands, deserts, mountains) or **aquatic** (in water — ponds, rivers, seas).

Living things have special features that help them survive in their habitat. These are called **adaptations**. Adaptations develop over a very long time, across many generations — not overnight in one animal.

**Desert (Thar, Rajasthan)** — hot days, cold nights, very little water.
- *Camel*: long legs keep the body away from hot sand; wide padded feet stop it sinking; long eyelashes and closable nostrils keep out sand; it can go days without drinking and passes little urine.
- *Cactus*: leaves reduced to **spines** (less water lost); thick fleshy green stem stores water and makes food; waxy coat; long roots.

**Mountains (Himalaya)** — very cold, snow, thin air.
- *Pine and deodar trees*: **cone shape** with sloping branches so snow slides off; needle-like leaves.
- *Yak and snow leopard*: thick fur, fat layer; snow leopard's wide furry paws act like snowshoes. Mountain goats have strong hooves for rocky slopes.

**Water (ponds, sea)**
- *Fish*: streamlined body, fins, **gills** to breathe oxygen dissolved in water, slippery scales.
- *Lotus and water lily*: leaves float, with waxy upper surfaces; stems are hollow and spongy.

**Grassland and forest** — a deer has long ears and eyes on the sides of the head to watch for danger and strong legs to sprint; a tiger has striped fur that blends with tall grass (**camouflage**).

Adaptation — feature that helps survival in a habitat
Terrestrial — on land
Aquatic — in water
Camouflage — blending with surroundings

check.q: Why are the leaves of a cactus turned into spines?
check.why: Spines have very little surface area, so far less water escapes from the plant in the dry desert.

sections.h: Why diversity matters — and how we protect it
sections.md:
Every species is a thread in a great web. Bees pollinate mustard and mango flowers; birds spread seeds; earthworms make soil fertile; frogs eat insects that would damage crops. Remove too many threads and the web sags.

Diversity is threatened when forests are cut, wetlands filled, rivers polluted, and animals hunted. Habitat loss is the biggest danger: if a forest disappears, the animals that are adapted to it may have nowhere else to go.

India protects diversity through **national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves** — Jim Corbett, Kaziranga, Gir, the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve. Communities have done this for centuries too: **sacred groves** in Meghalaya, Kerala and Maharashtra are patches of forest protected by local tradition. The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan is famous for protecting khejri trees and blackbuck.

You can help: plant native trees; save water; avoid single-use plastic; never disturb nests.

> **Did you know?** Many Indian villages have prepared a People's Biodiversity Register, recording local plants, animals and traditional knowledge.

check.q: What is the biggest threat to biodiversity?
check.why: When forests, wetlands and grasslands are destroyed, the species adapted to them lose their homes and food.

sections.h: Project: your school's biodiversity register and herbarium
sections.md:
The chapter encourages you to become a record-keeper of the life around you. Here is how a class can do it.

**1. Biodiversity register.** Divide the school campus into zones (garden, playground edge, near the water tank). Each group visits its zone once a week at the same time and records:

| Date | Name (local + common) | Plant or animal | Where seen | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 July | Gudhal / hibiscus | Shrub | Gate | Red flowers, bees visiting |
| 3 July | Myna | Bird | Playground | Pair, walking on grass |

Ask elders and the school gardener for local names and uses — this traditional knowledge is part of biodiversity too.

**2. Herbarium.** A herbarium is a collection of dried, pressed plant parts. Collect only fallen leaves or small pieces with permission, never uprooting plants. Press each leaf between newspaper sheets under heavy books for a week. Stick it on a sheet and label: name, date, place, plant type (herb/shrub/tree), venation and — if you saw it — root type.

**3. Look for patterns.** After a month, count: how many herbs, shrubs, trees and climbers? How many leaves have reticulate versus parallel venation? Did new insects appear after the monsoon began? Make a bar graph.

**4. Share.** Display the register on the notice board and suggest actions — a bird bath, a patch of native flowering plants for butterflies, a no-plastic zone.

A register kept over years shows how life changes with seasons and with human activity. Scientists use such long records to spot species that are declining.

check.q: Which is the right way to collect a plant sample for a herbarium?
options: Take fallen leaves or a small piece with permission
check.why: Collecting fallen leaves or small samples with permission studies plants without harming them.

workedExamples.q: Classify a maize plant fully: plant type, venation, seed and root.
steps: Maize has a soft green stem and is not woody — it is a herb (a tall grass).
Its long leaves have veins side by side — parallel venation.
Its grain has one cotyledon — a monocot.
Parallel venation predicts fibrous roots, which is what we find.
workedExamples.answer: Herb, parallel venation, monocot, fibrous roots.

workedExamples.q: Predict the roots of a tulsi plant without digging.
steps: Look at a tulsi leaf against light: the veins form a net.
Reticulate venation usually goes with a taproot.

workedExamples.q: Explain two adaptations of a fish to aquatic life.
steps: Streamlined body reduces resistance so it swims easily.
Gills take in oxygen dissolved in water.
workedExamples.answer: Streamlined body and gills (also fins and slippery scales).

workedExamples.q: A soaked rajma seed splits into two halves. What venation and roots do you expect?
steps: Dicots usually have reticulate venation and taproots.

summary: Biodiversity is the variety of living things on Earth.
We group living things by shared features to study them.
Herbs are small with soft stems; shrubs are bushy and woody near the base; trees have one tall woody trunk.
Climbers grow up supports, often with tendrils; creepers spread along the ground.
Venation is the pattern of veins: reticulate (net) or parallel.
Taproot = one main root with laterals; fibrous = bunch of similar roots.
Reticulate venation usually goes with taproots; parallel with fibrous roots.
Dicot seeds have two cotyledons; monocot seeds have one.
Dicots: reticulate + taproot; monocots: parallel + fibrous — patterns allow predictions.
Animals can be grouped by movement, food, body covering and habitat.
A habitat provides food, water, shelter; it can be terrestrial or aquatic.
Adaptations are features that help survival, developed over many generations.
Cactus, camel, pine, yak, fish and lotus each show adaptations to their habitat.
Habitat loss is the biggest threat to diversity; parks, sanctuaries and sacred groves protect it.
A biodiversity register and herbarium record local life over time.

glossary.d: Variety of plants, animals and other life in an area
Arrangement of veins in a leaf
Flat green blade of a leaf
Stalk joining leaf to stem
Seed leaf that stores food for the young plant
Collection of dried, pressed, labelled plant specimens
Feature suiting a living thing to its habitat

rd-school-c6-science.ch03-mindful-eating.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
rd-school-c6-science.ch03-mindful-eating.subtitle: What is really on your plate — and how a drop of iodine can reveal it

sections.md:
Ask five friends what they ate for lunch and you may get five different answers: rajma-chawal in Delhi, dal-baati in Jaipur, fish curry and rice in Kolkata, sambar-rice with rasam in Chennai, rice with bamboo-shoot curry in Shillong. India is a country of a thousand kitchens.

Why do people in different places eat differently? Mostly because of **what grows nearby**. Coastal Kerala and Bengal have plenty of coconut, rice and fish. Punjab's wheat fields make roti a daily food. Rajasthan's dry land grows bajra and jowar. Climate, local crops, culture, festivals and family traditions all shape our food.

Food habits also change over time. Our grandparents ate more **millets** like ragi, jowar and bajra; today many families eat more polished rice, wheat flour and packaged snacks. India even asked the world to celebrate 2023 as the **International Year of Millets**, because millets are nutritious and need little water.

But whatever the dish, one question matters: *does it give the body what it needs?* That is what **mindful eating** means — paying attention to what, how much and how we eat.

> **Did you know?** Ragi (finger millet) is very rich in calcium — far more than rice or wheat.

sections.h: Food then and now, here and there
sections.md:
The chapter asks you to become a food historian of your own family. Try this **survey**: ask a grandparent, a parent and yourself what you usually ate for breakfast, lunch and dinner at age 12.

| Who | Breakfast | Lunch | Dinner | Snacks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Grandmother (about 1965) | ragi porridge | rice, sambar, greens | jowar roti, dal | roasted groundnuts, seasonal fruit |
| Parent (about 1995) | idli or paratha | rice, dal, sabzi | roti, sabzi | biscuits, fruit |
| You (today) | bread, cornflakes | rice, dal, sabzi | roti, paneer | chips, noodles, cold drink |

(Your table will look different — that is the point!) Patterns many families notice:

- **Fewer millets and more refined grains** (white rice, maida).
- **More packaged and fried snacks**, with added sugar and salt.
- **Fewer seasonal and local foods** — today you can buy apples and peas all year, transported from far away.

**Seasonal and local eating.** Traditional diets followed the seasons: mangoes and cooling buttermilk in summer, sarson ka saag and makki roti in Punjab winters, sweet potatoes and til-gur laddoos around Makar Sankranti. Seasonal local food is usually fresher, cheaper, and travels a shorter distance, so it uses less fuel.

**Food also varies by occasion and by need.** Festivals bring special dishes; a sick person may get light khichdi; a mother feeding a baby needs extra nutrition.

No region's food is 'better' — each grew from local farms and wisdom. The goal is to keep the good parts of tradition (millets, pulses, greens, fermented foods like idli and curd) while avoiding too much of the new junk.

items.what: Millets, pulses, greens, seasonal fruit; home-cooked almost always
Rice and wheat dominate; some biscuits and bottled drinks appear
Packaged snacks, instant noodles, food delivery apps; millets returning
International Year of Millets promoted by India

fig.caption: How everyday eating has changed across three generations.

check.q: Why is eating seasonal, local food often a good idea?
options: It is fresher and travels a shorter distance
It is available only in packets
check.why: Seasonal local food is harvested nearby at the right time, so it is fresh and needs less transport.

sections.h: Nutrients: what food is made of
sections.md:
Food contains substances the body needs, called **nutrients**. There are five main groups, plus two helpers.

| Nutrient | Main job | Rich sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Carbohydrates** | Energy | Rice, wheat, millets, potato, sugar, banana |
| **Fats** | Energy (more than carbs per gram), stored energy | Ghee, oil, butter, nuts, milk |
| **Proteins** | Body-building, growth and repair | Dal, rajma, chana, milk, paneer, eggs, fish, meat, soybean |
| **Vitamins** | Protect from disease; keep eyes, skin, bones, gums healthy | Fruits, green leafy vegetables, milk |
| **Minerals** | Bones, teeth, blood, many body processes | Milk (calcium), leafy greens and jaggery (iron), iodised salt (iodine) |

Carbohydrates and fats are **energy-giving foods**; proteins are **body-building foods**; vitamins and minerals are **protective foods**.

Two more things are essential though they are not counted as nutrients in the same way:
- **Dietary fibre (roughage)** — the parts of plant food we can't digest, found in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, sprouts. It helps food move through the gut and prevents constipation.
- **Water** — helps digest food, carry nutrients, remove wastes in urine and sweat, and keep body temperature steady.

Most foods contain **more than one nutrient**. Milk has proteins, fats, carbohydrates (milk sugar), calcium and vitamins all together.

check.why: Carbohydrates and fats are the body's main fuels; fats give more energy per gram.

sections.md:
How do we know a potato has starch? Do the tests yourself (with a teacher).

**Test for starch**: Put a little of the food (or a potato slice) on a dish and add 2–3 drops of dilute **iodine solution**. A **blue-black** colour means starch is present.

**Test for fats**: Rub a little food (a peanut, a bit of ghee, crushed groundnut) on a piece of paper. Let it dry. If an **oily, translucent patch** appears that lets light through when held up, the food contains fat.

**Test for proteins**: Take a small amount of food in a test tube with water (or a little crushed food). Add 2 drops of **copper sulphate solution** and 10 drops of **sodium hydroxide** (caustic soda) solution. Shake. A **violet (purple)** colour shows protein.

| Food | Starch | Fat | Protein |
|---|---|---|---|
| Raw potato | ✔ | ✘ | little |
| Groundnut | little | ✔ | ✔ |
| Boiled egg white | ✘ | ✘ | ✔ |
| Rice | ✔ | ✘ | little |
| Milk | ✘ | ✔ | ✔ |

**Safety**: iodine stains; sodium hydroxide is caustic — wear gloves, use small amounts, never taste anything in the lab.

check.why: The violet colour in this test is the sign of proteins.

sections.md:
A **balanced diet** gives all the nutrients, roughage and water in the **right amounts** for a person's needs — not too little, not too much.

Needs differ. A growing 12-year-old needs plenty of protein and calcium. A farmer or athlete who does hard physical work needs more energy food than someone who sits at a desk. Pregnant women, the sick and elderly people have special needs.

A typical balanced Indian day might look like:
- **Breakfast**: poha with peanuts and vegetables, a glass of milk.
- **Lunch**: roti or rice, dal, a green vegetable, curd, salad.
- **Snack**: a fruit, roasted chana or a handful of nuts.
- **Dinner**: khichdi with vegetables, or millet roti with sabzi and dal.

Tips for mindful eating:
1. Eat a **variety** of colours — green, orange, red, yellow vegetables and fruits.
2. Prefer whole grains and millets; don't over-polish rice.
3. Don't overcook vegetables or wash them after cutting — vitamins are lost.
4. Eat slowly, chew well, and stop when you are full.
5. Drink clean water through the day.

**Junk food** — chips, sugary cold drinks, deep-fried snacks, instant noodles — is high in fat, sugar and salt but low in proteins, vitamins and fibre. Eating it often can lead to **obesity** and later to diabetes and heart problems. An occasional treat is fine; a daily habit is not.

check.q: Which is the BEST example of a balanced meal?
options: Rice, dal, green vegetable, curd and salad
check.why: That meal combines energy, protein, protective foods and fibre in sensible amounts.

sections.h: Eating mindfully: how, when and how much
sections.md:
Mindful eating is not only about *what* is on the plate. It is also about **how** we eat.

**Listen to your body.** Hunger and fullness are signals. Eating slowly gives the stomach time to tell the brain 'I'm full' — this message takes about 15–20 minutes to arrive. Gulping food in front of a screen often leads to overeating because we stop noticing these signals.

**Regular meals.** Skipping breakfast can leave you tired and unable to concentrate in class. Long gaps followed by big meals are harder on the body than regular, moderate meals.

**Portion sense.** A handy guide: about half the plate vegetables and fruit, a quarter grains (preferably whole grains or millets), a quarter pulses, milk products, eggs or other protein foods, with only a little oil, sugar and salt.

**Hidden sugar and salt.** One 300 mL bottle of a sweetened cold drink can contain around 30 g of sugar — about 7 to 8 teaspoons. Packaged chips and namkeen are often very salty. Too much sugar harms teeth and adds empty energy; too much salt is linked with high blood pressure later in life.

**Water first.** When thirsty, choose plain water, buttermilk, nimbu-pani with little sugar, or coconut water instead of sweet bottled drinks.

**Activity matters too.** Food gives energy; play, walking, cycling and sports use it. Health comes from balance between the two — at least an hour of active play a day is a good aim for children.

**A mindful-eating checklist:** Did I wash my hands? Is my plate colourful? Am I eating slowly, without a screen? Did I stop when comfortably full? Did I waste any food?

check.q: Why does eating slowly help prevent overeating?
options: The 'I'm full' signal from stomach to brain takes time to arrive
check.why: Fullness signals take around 15–20 minutes to reach the brain, so eating slowly lets you notice them before you eat too much.

sections.md:
If the diet lacks one or more nutrients for a long time, a **deficiency disease** can develop. These diseases can be prevented by eating a balanced diet.

| Missing | Disease / condition | Signs |
|---|---|---|
| Vitamin A | Night blindness, poor vision | Difficulty seeing in dim light |
| Vitamin B1 | Beriberi | Weak muscles, little energy |
| Vitamin C | Scurvy | Bleeding gums, slow healing of wounds |
| Vitamin D | Rickets | Soft, bent bones |
| Calcium | Weak bones and teeth | Bones break easily |
| Iron | Anaemia | Tiredness, pale skin |
| Iodine | Goitre | Swollen neck (thyroid gland) |

Lack of protein and energy over a long time causes **malnutrition**, where children stop growing well and fall ill easily. India's mid-day meal scheme (PM POSHAN) gives school children cooked meals partly to fight this.

The cures are often simple: carrots, papaya and green leafy vegetables for vitamin A; amla, guava, lemon and oranges for vitamin C; sunlight on the skin for vitamin D; **iodised salt** for iodine; jaggery, green leafy vegetables and pulses for iron. (Anyone with symptoms should see a doctor.)

> **Did you know?** Long ago, sailors on long voyages got scurvy until it was found that citrus fruits prevent it.

check.q: Bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds suggest a lack of:
check.why: These are signs of scurvy, which is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

sections.md:
Mindful eating also means caring about **how food reaches us**. Wash hands before eating. Keep food covered from flies. Don't waste — every grain of rice took water, soil, sunlight and a farmer's work. Take only as much as you will eat.

Packaged foods have a **label**. Learn to read it: check the expiry date, look for added sugar and salt, and look for the green dot (vegetarian) or brown dot (non-vegetarian) symbol, and the FSSAI licence number which shows the food business is registered.

Finally, enjoy food together. Eating with family, without screens, helps you notice when you're full and makes meals happier.

check.q: Which practice reduces vitamin loss from vegetables?
options: Washing before cutting and cooking briefly
Throwing away the cooking water always
check.why: Washing before cutting and not overcooking keeps more of the water-soluble vitamins in the food.

parts.md: Arjun, twelve, from Nagpur, loved chips and cola. Every afternoon after school he grabbed a packet and a bottle and sat with his phone. By the evening match he was always tired, and at the school sports trial he ran out of breath halfway round the track. His coach, Mrs D'Souza, noticed. 'Try an experiment,' she said. 'For one week, keep a food diary — and try to make your plate show at least four colours every meal.'

Arjun was doubtful, but he loved experiments. Monday: green palak dal, white rice, orange carrot salad, yellow mango. Tuesday: brown ragi dosa, red tomato chutney, white curd. He swapped the cola for buttermilk and the chips for roasted chana. He also tried the 'no phone at the table' rule his grandmother suggested and was surprised to find he felt full sooner.

By Sunday his diary was full of colours — and a few honest notes: *Wednesday: had samosas at a party.* Mrs D'Souza laughed. 'One treat is fine. Look at the pattern, not one day.' At the next trial Arjun finished the lap without stopping. It wasn't magic; a week is short, and sleep and practice helped too. But he had learnt to notice what he ate — and that, his coach said, was the real beginning of mindful eating.

workedExamples.q: Riya often feels tired and her palms look pale. Which nutrient may be lacking and what can she eat?
steps: Tiredness and pale skin are signs of anaemia.
Anaemia is caused mostly by lack of iron.
Iron-rich foods: green leafy vegetables, jaggery, pulses, dates.
workedExamples.answer: Iron; she should eat spinach, jaggery, dal and similar foods (and see a doctor).

workedExamples.q: Plan a vegetarian tiffin with energy, protein and protective foods.
steps: Energy: two rotis or a millet chilla.
Protein: paneer bhurji or sprouted moong.
Protective: cucumber-carrot salad and a guava.

workedExamples.q: A drop of iodine on bread turns blue-black, but on cooking oil it stays brown. Interpret.
steps: No colour change means no starch.
workedExamples.answer: Bread contains starch; oil does not (oil is fat).

workedExamples.q: A 300 mL cold drink has 30 g sugar. One teaspoon holds about 4 g. How many teaspoons is that?

summary: Food habits vary across India due to local crops, climate and culture.
Diets have changed over generations: fewer millets, more packaged food.
Seasonal, local food is fresh and travels less.
Nutrients: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals.
Carbs and fats give energy; proteins build the body; vitamins and minerals protect.
Roughage and water are essential for digestion and body functions.
Starch + iodine → blue-black; fat leaves an oily patch on paper; protein → violet with copper sulphate and caustic soda.
A balanced diet has all nutrients in the right amounts for a person's needs.
Eat slowly, regularly and without screens; stop when comfortably full.
Watch hidden sugar and salt in packaged foods and drinks.
Deficiency diseases: scurvy (vit C), rickets (vit D), night blindness (vit A), beriberi (vit B1), anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine).
Junk food is high in fat, sugar, salt and low in nutrients.
Don't overcook or wash vegetables after cutting.
Read food labels; avoid waste; eat mindfully.

Poor health due to wrong or too little food

rd-school-c6-science.ch04-magnets.title: Exploring Magnets
rd-school-c6-science.ch04-magnets.subtitle: An invisible pull that guided sailors, sorts scrap and sticks notes to your fridge

sections.md:
An old story told in many countries goes like this: a shepherd named Magnes was walking on a hillside when the iron nails in his sandals and the iron tip of his stick suddenly clung to a black rock. That rock was **magnetite**, a natural magnet. Whether the story is true or a legend, people in ancient Greece, China and India did know of rocks that attract iron. These are called **natural magnets** or lodestones ("leading stones").

Today we use **artificial magnets** made of iron, steel or special alloys, shaped as **bar magnets, horseshoe (U-shaped) magnets, ring magnets, button and disc magnets**, and even flexible fridge-magnet sheets. You'll find magnets in speakers, earphones, motors, pencil boxes, cupboard doors, toys and MRI machines in hospitals.

In this chapter you'll learn which things a magnet attracts, what its **poles** are, how a magnet finds **direction**, how magnets **attract and repel** each other, and how to make and care for magnets.

check.q: What is magnetite?
options: A natural magnet found in rocks
check.why: Magnetite is a naturally occurring rock that attracts iron, which is why it is called a natural magnet or lodestone.

sections.md:
Bring a magnet near a heap of things: an iron nail, a steel spoon, a coin, an eraser, a pencil, a plastic scale, an aluminium foil, a glass bangle, a key, paper clips.

Materials that a magnet **attracts** are **magnetic materials** — iron, nickel, cobalt and alloys like steel. Materials not attracted are **non-magnetic** — wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, cloth, and most metals like copper, aluminium, gold and silver.

Important: **not every metal is magnetic!** An aluminium vessel or copper wire will not stick. And some Indian coins may or may not stick depending on what metal they are made of — test and see.

**Record your results:**

| Object | Material | Attracted? |
|---|---|---|
| Nail | Iron | Yes |
| Spoon | Steel | Usually yes |
| Scale | Plastic | No |
| Foil | Aluminium | No |
| Pencil | Wood + graphite | No |
| Key | Steel or brass | Depends — test! |

A cool use: in scrap yards, huge **electromagnets** on cranes lift iron scrap and separate it from other waste. In the kitchen, a magnet can find iron filings mixed with sand. Some breakfast cereals 'fortified with iron' contain tiny iron particles that a strong magnet can pull out of a soggy mash!

check.q: Which object will a magnet attract?
check.why: Steel is mostly iron, a magnetic material; aluminium, copper and glass are non-magnetic.

sections.md:
Spread iron filings (or tiny pins) on paper and roll a bar magnet through them. Lift it. You'll see thick clusters of filings near the **two ends** and very few in the middle. The two regions where the attraction is strongest are the **poles** of the magnet.

Every magnet has **two poles**: a **North pole (N)** and a **South pole (S)**. Even a ring or disc magnet has two — on its two faces.

Here is something surprising: if you break a bar magnet into two pieces, you don't get a lone N and a lone S. **Each piece becomes a complete magnet with its own N and S.** Break it again — the same happens. Magnetic poles always come in pairs.

**Seeing the invisible.** Put a sheet of paper over a bar magnet and sprinkle iron filings on it. Tap the paper gently. The filings arrange themselves in curved lines from one pole to the other — a picture of the magnet's **magnetic field**, the region around it where it can act.

North-seeking pole — end that points north
Magnetic field — region around a magnet where it acts

check.q: A bar magnet is broken into three pieces. How many poles does each piece have?
check.why: Every piece of a magnet, however small, becomes a complete magnet with a north and a south pole.

sections.md:
Hang a bar magnet from its middle with a thread so it can turn freely, away from iron objects. Wait until it stops. Mark the direction. Turn it and let go again. It **always comes to rest in the north–south direction.** The end pointing north is the **north-seeking pole** (N); the other is the **south-seeking pole** (S).

Why? Because the **Earth itself behaves like a giant magnet**, and a freely suspended magnet lines up with it.

This property gave humans the **magnetic compass**: a small, light magnetised needle pivoted so it can spin, inside a case with directions marked. Its north end is usually painted red. To use it, turn the compass box until the N marking sits under the needle's red end; now you can read all directions.

Sailors, travellers through deserts, mountaineers and soldiers have relied on compasses for centuries. Ancient Chinese sources describe early direction-finders made with lodestone; the floating magnetised "fish" is one such device mentioned by historians.

**Make your own compass**: stroke a sewing needle about 30 times in one direction with one pole of a magnet. Push it through a small piece of cork or a leaf, float it on water in a bowl (non-steel). It will slowly turn to point north–south.

check.q: A freely suspended bar magnet always rests pointing:
check.why: It aligns with the Earth's magnetism, so it settles in the north–south direction.

sections.md:
Take two bar magnets. Bring the N of one near the N of the other: they **push apart**. Try S near S: they push apart again. Now N near S: they **snap together**.

**Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.**

This gives us a reliable test: *repulsion is the sure test of a magnet.* Why? Because an iron bar that isn't a magnet will be **attracted** by both poles of a magnet — so attraction alone can't tell you whether the bar is magnetised. Only a magnet can **repel** another magnet.

You can even make a car move without touching it: tape a magnet on a toy car; bring a like pole close behind and it rolls away.

**Floating ring magnets.** Slide several ring magnets onto a pencil held upright, with like poles facing each other. The rings float above one another with gaps, held apart by repulsion — a striking classroom demonstration.

check.q: You have an iron bar and a magnet that look the same. The surest test is:
options: Check which repels a known magnet
check.why: Only a magnet can repel another magnet; iron is just attracted by both poles.

sections.h: Pulling through things and across gaps
sections.md:
Does a magnet need to touch an object to attract it? Try these investigations.

**1. Through materials.** Place a paper clip on a sheet of paper and move a magnet *below* the sheet. The clip follows! Repeat with a thin wooden board, a plastic tray, a glass plate and a steel plate.

| Sheet between | Does the clip move? |
|---|---|
| Paper | Yes |
| Cardboard | Yes |
| Thin wood | Yes (if not too thick) |
| Glass | Yes |
| Steel plate | Weakly or not at all |

Magnets act **through non-magnetic materials**. A steel sheet behaves differently because it is itself magnetic and 'soaks up' the magnet's effect.

**2. Across a gap.** Place a pin on the table and slowly slide a magnet towards it along a ruler. Note the distance at which the pin first jumps to the magnet. Try with a stronger magnet: the distance is larger. A magnet's pull becomes **weaker with distance**.

**3. Comparing strength fairly.** To compare two magnets, keep the same pin, same table and same starting distance, and change only the magnet — a fair test! Another way: count how many paper clips each magnet can hold in a hanging chain.

**Fun uses:** a magnetic 'fishing' game (paper fish with clips, a stick with a magnet), a puppet that dances on a cardboard stage while a magnet moves beneath it, or a maze where you guide a steel ball with a magnet from below.

fig.caption: A magnet's pull passes through cardboard, so the clip follows the hidden magnet.
fig.alt: Paper clip moving on top of a sheet as a magnet moves underneath

check.q: A pin jumps to a magnet only when the magnet is 2 cm away. With a stronger magnet, this distance will most likely be:
check.why: A stronger magnet's pull reaches further before becoming too weak, so the pin jumps from a greater distance.

sections.md:
**Making a magnet (single-touch method)**: Lay an iron nail or steel strip on a table. Place one pole of a bar magnet at one end and slide it along to the other end. Lift the magnet up high, bring it back to the starting end, and repeat in the **same direction** with the **same pole** 30–40 times. Test with pins — your nail is now a weak magnet. Rubbing back and forth would undo the work.

**Magnets lose their magnetism** if they are:
- heated strongly,
- hammered or dropped from a height again and again,
- stored carelessly near each other (like poles together).

**Storing magnets**: keep bar magnets in pairs with **unlike poles side by side**, separated by a piece of wood, with a soft iron strip (a **keeper**) across the ends. Horseshoe magnets get a keeper across their poles.

Keep magnets away from phones, credit/debit cards, computers, CDs and mechanical watches — they can damage them.

> **Did you know?** Some trains in China and Japan float above their tracks using powerful magnets — maglev, short for magnetic levitation.

check.q: Which action will weaken a magnet?
check.why: Repeated hammering or dropping disturbs the magnet's arrangement and makes it lose magnetism.

sections.md:
Look around your home and town — magnets are quietly doing jobs everywhere.

- **Refrigerator doors** have a flexible magnetic strip in the rubber seal, which pulls the door shut and keeps cold air in.
- **Pencil boxes, bags and cupboard latches** use small magnets as catches.
- **Speakers and earphones** contain magnets that, with electric currents, make a cone vibrate and produce sound.
- **Electric motors** in fans, mixers and washing machines use magnets to turn.
- **Hospitals** use MRI machines with very strong magnets to take detailed pictures inside the body (that is why patients remove metal objects first).
- **Recycling plants** use magnets to separate iron and steel from mixed waste.
- **Tailors** use a magnet to collect dropped pins from the floor — a quick, practical trick.

**Earth's magnet and migrating animals.** Scientists have found evidence that some birds, sea turtles and fish sense the Earth's magnetism and use it, along with the Sun and stars, to find their way on long journeys. How exactly they do it is still being studied.

**A caution:** small, powerful magnets are dangerous if swallowed — keep them away from little children.

check.q: Why does a refrigerator door close tightly on its own?
options: A magnetic strip in its seal pulls it to the steel body
check.why: A flexible magnetic strip inside the door seal is attracted to the steel body of the fridge, pulling the door shut.

parts.md: On a school trek in Himachal, fog rolled in and the trail markers vanished. Meera's group stopped, worried. Their teacher's phone had no signal. Meera remembered the sewing kit in her bag and the fridge magnet from her pencil box.

She stroked a needle thirty times in one direction with the magnet, pierced a dry leaf with it and floated it in a steel-free plastic tiffin lid of water. Slowly the needle swung and settled. Their map said the camp lay to the north-east. Keeping the needle in view at every turn, they walked carefully and reached the camp as the fog lifted. The teacher grinned: "That's science you can trust."

workedExamples.q: A magnet attracts a nail with both its poles. Is the nail a magnet?
steps: If the nail were a magnet, one of the magnet's poles would repel one end.
Both poles attract, so there is no repulsion.
workedExamples.answer: No — the nail is just magnetic material, not a magnet.

workedExamples.q: Bar magnet A's unknown end repels the N pole of a labelled magnet. Name that end.
steps: It repels N, so it must be N.

workedExamples.q: Which arrangement stores two bar magnets safely?
steps: Place them side by side with N next to S.
Put wood between them and keepers across the ends.
workedExamples.answer: Unlike poles side by side with keepers.

workedExamples.q: Magnet X holds a chain of 6 clips; magnet Y holds 11. Which is stronger and how do you keep the test fair?
steps: More clips held means stronger pull.
Use identical clips and hang them the same way from the same pole type.
workedExamples.answer: Y is stronger; keep clips and method identical.

summary: Magnetite is a natural magnet; most magnets we use are artificial.
Magnets come as bar, horseshoe, ring, disc and button shapes.
Iron, nickel, cobalt and steel are magnetic; wood, plastic, copper, aluminium are not.
Attraction is strongest at the two poles.
Poles always come in pairs; broken pieces are full magnets.
Iron filings reveal the magnetic field around a magnet.
A freely suspended magnet rests north–south; the Earth acts like a giant magnet.
A compass uses a magnetised needle to find direction.
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract; repulsion is the sure test of a magnet.
Magnets act through non-magnetic materials and weaken with distance.
Magnets can be made by stroking iron in one direction.
Heating, hammering and dropping weaken magnets; store with keepers.
Magnets work in fridges, speakers, motors, MRI machines and recycling.

rd-school-c6-science.ch05-measurement-mo.title: Measurement of Length and Motion
rd-school-c6-science.ch05-measurement-mo.subtitle: From handspans to metres, and from a rolling ball to a spinning fan

sections.md:
Deepa and her brother Arjun want to know if a new table will fit through the door. Deepa measures it with her handspan: **8 spans**. Arjun, who is older, gets **6½ spans**. Who is right? Both — and neither! Their hands are different sizes.

For thousands of years people measured with body parts: the **handspan**, the **cubit** (elbow to fingertip), the **foot**, the **pace** (a step), the **angul** (finger width). Ancient Indian texts mention units like angula and dhanush, and the Harappan cities had remarkably standard bricks and measuring scales — they clearly cared about measuring well.

The trouble with body units is that **they differ from person to person**. Trade, building and science need units that mean exactly the same thing everywhere. That's why we use **standard units**.

**Try it in class:** let five students measure the length of the teacher's table in handspans and write the results on the board. You will probably get five different numbers — the best possible proof that we need a common unit.

check.q: Why did Deepa and Arjun get different answers for the same table?
options: Their handspans are of different lengths
One of them counted wrongly on purpose
check.why: A handspan is not a standard unit; different people's hands are different sizes, so the count changes.

sections.md:
Measurement is one of humanity's oldest sciences.

- **Harappan civilisation (about 4,500 years ago):** archaeologists found a finely marked scale made of shell at Mohenjo-daro and one of ivory at Lothal in Gujarat, with very small, even divisions. Harappan bricks across many cities had the same proportions (length : breadth : thickness about 4 : 2 : 1), showing standardised measurement.
- **Traditional Indian units:** old texts describe a chain of units built from the body — *angula* (finger width), *vitasti* (span), *hasta* (cubit, roughly the forearm length), *dhanush* (bow length) and *yojana* for long distances. Their exact values varied by region and period, which is exactly the problem standard units solve.
- **Markets of the past:** cloth was often sold by the *gaj* (yard) — measured on a merchant's arm or rod — and land by local units that differed from one district to another, causing disputes.
- **The metric system (1790s, France):** scientists defined the metre as a fixed fraction of the distance from the North Pole to the Equator, and made a metal rod to keep as the standard. Today the metre is defined, even more exactly, using the speed of light.
- **India goes metric:** India adopted the metric system by law in the 1950s and switched gradually during the 1960s; old units like the *ser* and *maund* slowly disappeared from markets (some, like the *gaj* and *bigha*, are still heard in everyday speech).

The big idea: a unit is useful only if **everyone agrees** on it.

items.what: Harappan scales at Mohenjo-daro and Lothal; standard bricks
Angula, vitasti, hasta, dhanush, yojana — body-based units
Metric system created in France; the metre defined
International System of Units (SI) adopted worldwide
India switches to metric units

fig.caption: From finger widths to the SI metre.

check.q: Why were standard units needed?
options: Body units differ from person to person, causing confusion
check.why: Units based on body parts give different results for different people, so trade, building and science needed units that are the same for everyone.

sections.h: Standard units and the SI system
sections.md:
To **measure** means to compare an unknown quantity with a known fixed quantity called the **unit**. The result has two parts: a **number** and a **unit** — "2.5 metres". A number alone ("2.5") is meaningless.

Today almost the whole world uses the **International System of Units (SI)**. The SI unit of length is the **metre (m)**.

| Unit | Symbol | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| kilometre | km | 1 km = 1000 m |
| metre | m | base unit |
| centimetre | cm | 1 m = 100 cm |
| millimetre | mm | 1 cm = 10 mm |

So 1 m = 1000 mm. Use km for distances between cities (Delhi to Agra ≈ 230 km by road), m for a cricket pitch (about 20 m between the stumps), cm for your book, mm for the thickness of a coin.

**Writing units correctly:** use the symbols without a full stop and without adding 's' for plural — write 5 m, not 5 m. or 5 ms; leave a space between number and unit; the symbol for kilometre is small k: km.

fig.caption: Start from any clear mark if the zero is broken, and subtract.
fig.alt: Ruler with a bar growing from 1 cm to 5.5 cm

check.q: How many millimetres are in 3.2 cm?

sections.md:
A scale is useless if used carelessly. Rules for accurate measuring:

1. **Place the scale along** (in contact with) the length to be measured, not tilted.
2. If the zero mark is worn or broken, start from **another full mark** (say 1 cm) and subtract it from the final reading.
3. Keep your **eye exactly above** the point being read. Looking from the side gives a wrong reading — an error called **parallax**.
4. Read to the smallest division your scale shows (usually 1 mm).
5. Repeat a few times and take the **average**.

**Measuring a curved line**: use a **thread**. Lay it carefully along the curve, mark the ends, straighten it on a scale. For your waist, the girth of a tree or a bangle, a **measuring tape** (as used by tailors) works the same way.

**Choosing the right tool:** a 15 cm or 30 cm ruler for a notebook; a metre scale for a door; a measuring tape for a room, a tree trunk or your height; a long surveyor's tape or a measuring wheel for a playground or a road. Today surveyors also use laser distance meters and satellite positioning.

check.q: Viewing the scale from an angle while reading causes:
check.why: Reading from the side shifts where the mark appears to be — that's parallax; look straight down instead.

sections.h: Activity: measuring yourself and your classroom
sections.md:
Let us put the rules into practice.

**1. Your height.** Stand barefoot with your back flat against a wall, heels together. A friend places a book flat on your head, touching the wall, and marks the wall under it with a pencil. Measure from floor to mark with a tape. Repeat three times and average.

**2. Your handspan and foot length in cm.** Now your body units become useful *because* you know their standard value. If your handspan is 16 cm, a table of 8 spans is about 8 × 16 = 128 cm.

**3. The classroom.** Measure length and breadth with a measuring tape. If the tape is shorter than the room, mark where it ends with chalk and continue from there, adding the parts.

**4. Estimate first, then measure.** Write a guess for each before measuring; compare. With practice your estimates improve — a valuable skill for engineers, tailors and carpenters.

**Sample record:**

| Thing | Estimate | Measured (avg of 3) |
|---|---|---|
| My height | 140 cm | 146.2 cm |
| Classroom length | 8 m | 9.35 m |
| Notebook width | 15 cm | 17.4 cm |
| Bangle circumference (thread) | 15 cm | 17.8 cm |

**Discuss:** why did the three height readings differ a little? (Posture, how the book was held, reading the tape.) This is why scientists repeat measurements and average them.

check.q: Your three readings of a bench are 152.1 cm, 151.9 cm and 152.3 cm. The best value is:

sections.md:
Look out of a moving train window. Trees seem to run backwards; your friend opposite seems still. Is your friend moving?

An object is in **motion** if its **position changes with time** compared to a **reference point** (something taken as fixed). It is at **rest** if its position does not change with respect to that reference.

Your friend is at rest compared to the train, but in motion compared to the trees. **Rest and motion are relative** — always say "with respect to what".

**Describing position.** To say where something is, we need three things: a **reference point**, a **distance** and a **direction**. "The post office is 300 m east of the school gate." "The milestone says Agra 45 km" — the reference point is Agra, the distance 45 km. On the same road, a second milestone reading 40 km a few minutes later tells you that you have moved 5 km closer to Agra — your position has changed with time, so you are in motion.

**Even 'still' things move.** A house seems at rest relative to the ground, but the Earth spins and goes around the Sun, carrying the house with it. Everything depends on the reference you choose.

check.q: A passenger sits in a moving bus. Relative to the bus driver, the passenger is:
check.why: The passenger's position does not change with respect to the driver, so relative to the driver they are at rest.

sections.md:
Watch the world and you'll spot different kinds of motion.

| Type | What happens | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Linear (rectilinear)** | Moves along a straight line | March-past soldiers, a ball rolling straight, a falling stone, a train on a straight track |
| **Circular** | Moves along a circle, distance from a centre stays the same | A stone whirled on a thread, the tip of a ceiling fan blade, a giant wheel seat |
| **Periodic (oscillatory)** | Repeats itself after fixed intervals of time | A swing, a pendulum, heartbeat, a see-saw, guitar string |

(Some motions also spin about their own axis — a top, the Earth turning — called **rotational** motion.)

Objects can show **more than one** motion at once. A bicycle wheel rotates while the cycle moves in a straight line. The Earth spins on its axis and goes around the Sun. A pendulum swinging repeats at regular intervals — that's periodic, and its bob moves along part of a circle.

A **pendulum's** regular swing was used in old clocks to keep time. Circular motion that repeats — like the hands of a clock or the Moon going round the Earth — is also periodic.

fig.caption: Linear, circular and periodic motion side by side.
fig.alt: Ball rolling straight, stone circling, pendulum swinging

keyTerms: Reference point — fixed point used to describe position
Linear motion — along a straight line
Circular motion — along a circular path
Periodic motion — repeats after equal time intervals

check.q: The motion of a child on a swing is:
check.why: The swing goes to and fro, repeating itself after a fixed time — periodic motion.

sections.md:
Let us practise identifying motions in familiar scenes.

| Scene | Motion(s) |
|---|---|
| A car on a straight highway | Linear (car body); rotational (wheels) |
| A merry-go-round at a mela | Circular (and periodic, as it repeats) |
| A sewing-machine needle | Periodic (up and down) |
| A child sliding down a straight slide | Linear |
| The blades of a ceiling fan | Circular / rotational, periodic |
| A plucked sitar string | Periodic (vibration) |
| A ball thrown to a friend | Neither straight nor circular — a curved path |
| Earth | Spinning on its axis (once a day) and going round the Sun (once a year) — both periodic |

**Time from periodic motion.** Because periodic motions repeat at steady intervals, humans have used them to measure time: day and night (Earth's spin), the lunar month (Moon's phases), the year (Earth round the Sun), the pendulum clock, and today quartz crystals vibrating in watches.

**Try it: your own pendulum.** Tie a small stone to a 50 cm thread, hang it from a nail and set it swinging. Count the swings in 30 seconds using a clock. Shorten the thread to 25 cm and count again. What do you notice? (Shorter pendulums swing faster.) Keep everything else the same so it is a fair test!

fig.caption: The Earth spins on its axis and travels around the Sun at the same time.
fig.alt: A blue Earth spinning while moving along an elliptical path around a yellow Sun

check.q: Which motion helped people measure a 'day'?
options: The Earth spinning on its axis
check.why: One full spin of the Earth on its axis makes one day and night, a periodic motion used to measure time.

parts.md: In a narrow lane of Lucknow, Salim Bhai's tailoring shop smelled of starch and new cloth. Twelve-year-old Kavya came with her mother to get a kurta stitched for Eid celebrations at her friend's house. Salim Bhai looped his yellow tape round her shoulders, waist and arms, calling out numbers that his son wrote down: 'Shoulder 34, length 82, sleeve 48...'

'Why not just use your hand?' Kavya asked, remembering her science class. Salim Bhai laughed. 'My father measured with his arm — one *gaj* was from his nose to his fingertip. When customers came back, his arm was the same, so it worked for him. But when I sent cloth to a workshop in Delhi, their *gaj* was different! The kurtas came back too short. Since then, only centimetres.' He tapped the tape: on one side inches, on the other centimetres.

As he worked, Kavya watched the sewing machine: the wheel went round and round, the needle bobbed up and down, and the cloth slid straight forward. 'Circular, periodic and linear motion — all at once!' she said. Salim Bhai raised his eyebrows. 'Is that what it's called? I only know that if the needle loses its rhythm, the stitches go crooked.' 'That's because periodic motion keeps a steady interval,' Kavya said proudly. A week later the kurta fit perfectly — every centimetre where it should be.

Convert 2.75 km into metres and centimetres.
A cloth is 6 handspans long. If one handspan is 18 cm, what is its length in metres?
Three readings of a table length are 120.2 cm, 120.4 cm and 120.3 cm. Give the best value.
A milestone reads 'Jaipur 62 km'. Twenty minutes later another reads 'Jaipur 47 km'. How far did the bus travel, and was it in motion relative to Jaipur?
steps: Its distance from Jaipur changed with time, so it was in motion relative to Jaipur.

summary: Body units like handspan and cubit vary from person to person.
Harappans used finely marked scales; India adopted the metric system in the 1950s–60s.
Measurement = comparing with a standard unit; result = number + unit.
SI unit of length is the metre.
Place the scale along the object, eye directly above the mark (avoid parallax).
With a broken zero, start from a full mark and subtract.
Use a thread or tape for curved lengths; repeat readings and average.
Motion = change in position with time relative to a reference point.
Position needs a reference point, distance and direction.
Rest and motion are relative.
Linear motion is along a straight line; circular along a circle; periodic repeats in equal intervals.
An object can have more than one type of motion at the same time.
Periodic motions are used to measure time.
practice: Why are handspan and cubit not reliable units?
Name two pieces of evidence that the Harappans measured carefully.
Convert: 7.5 m to cm; 450 mm to cm; 3 km 250 m to m.
Describe how you would measure the length of a curved line on a map.
List four precautions while measuring length with a scale.
Describe how to measure your height accurately at home.
Classify: hands of a clock, a bouncing ball, a train on straight rails, a pendulum, the Earth's spin.
Explain with an example how an object can be at rest and in motion at the same time.
What is a reference point? Give an example.
A bicycle moves on a road. What types of motion do its wheel and frame show?
Plan a fair test to see whether a pendulum's length changes how many swings it makes in 30 seconds.

rd-school-c6-science.ch06-materials.title: Materials Around Us
rd-school-c6-science.ch06-materials.subtitle: Why a tumbler can be glass, steel or plastic — but never paper-thin sugar

sections.md:
Open your kitchen cupboard. A steel tumbler, a glass tumbler, a plastic tumbler, maybe a copper lota and a clay kulhad. They are all the **same object** — something to drink from — but made of **different materials**.

Now look the other way: steel makes tumblers, spoons, cupboards, railway tracks and bridges. One material, many objects.

An **object** is a thing with a definite shape and use. A **material** is what it is made of. Wood, glass, plastic, metal, cotton, paper, clay, rubber, leather, stone — all materials.

Why is a frying pan metal and not plastic? Why are windows glass and not wood? The answer lies in **properties** — the qualities of a material that make it suitable for a job. Learning those properties lets you choose like an engineer.

> **Did you know?** The iron pillar at Mehrauli in Delhi is about 1,600 years old and has resisted rusting remarkably well — a famous puzzle of ancient Indian metalwork that scientists still study.

check.q: A steel tumbler and a steel spoon show that:
options: One object can be made of many materials
One material can make many objects
check.why: Both very different objects are made of the same material, steel.

sections.md:
Why sort? Grouping objects by properties makes them easy to find (think of a grocery shop with rice, pulses and spices in separate aisles), and helps us study them.

We can group objects in many ways: by **material** (wooden things, metal things), by **use** (things to eat with, things to write with), by **shape** (round, flat), or by a **property** (hard or soft, shiny or dull).

A single object can belong to different groups depending on the rule you pick. A steel spoon is in the group "metal objects", "shiny objects", "hard objects" and "things used for eating". Always state your rule first.

**Natural or human-made?** Another useful grouping: some materials come straight from nature — wood, cotton, wool, clay, stone, jute, silk; others are made by people from natural substances — plastic, glass, steel, paper, nylon, cement. Even 'human-made' materials start from nature: glass from sand, paper from wood pulp, steel from iron ore.

check.q: Which of these is a material, not an object?
check.why: Wood is what things are made of; chair, bottle and bucket are objects.

sections.md:
Freshly cut metals such as iron, copper, aluminium, gold and silver have a **shine**, called **lustre**. Materials with lustre are **lustrous**; wood, paper, clay and cloth are **non-lustrous** (dull).

Metals often lose their shine over time because air and moisture act on the surface — iron rusts brownish, copper vessels turn dull green-brown, silver anklets blacken. Rub the surface with sandpaper or a scrubber and the shine returns underneath. That's why your family polishes copper and brass utensils before Diwali.

Shine is used in jewellery (gold, silver), decorations and reflectors.

check.q: An old iron nail looks dull. When rubbed with sandpaper it shines. This shows:
options: Metals are lustrous but their surface can get dull
check.why: Fresh metal is lustrous; the dull layer formed by air and moisture is removed by rubbing.

sections.md:
Press or scratch materials with your fingernail or a key. A piece of sponge or cotton is easily pressed — it is **soft**. Iron, stone or glass cannot be scratched easily — they are **hard**.

Hardness decides use: we make tools, knives, buildings and floors from hard materials; pillows, mattresses and cushions from soft ones. **Diamond** is the hardest natural material and is used to cut glass.

Metals vary too: sodium is so soft it can be cut with a knife (only in labs, under kerosene — it reacts violently with water!), while iron is hard.

**Compare by scratching:** a material that can scratch another is the harder one. A steel nail scratches a piece of chalk, so steel is harder than chalk. Glass scratches copper; diamond scratches glass.

check.q: Which material is best for a cushion?
check.why: Foam is soft and compressible, making it comfortable for a cushion.

sections.md:
Put a spoonful of sugar in a glass of water and stir. It disappears! Sugar has **dissolved** — it is **soluble** in water. Salt, lemon juice, vinegar are also soluble.

Try sand, chalk powder, sawdust, oil: they don't disappear however long you stir. They are **insoluble**.

What about liquids? Vinegar and lemon juice **mix** completely with water (miscible); **oil and water** do not mix — oil forms a separate layer on top.

Gases dissolve too: **oxygen dissolved in water** lets fish and plants live underwater. Fizzy drinks have carbon dioxide dissolved under pressure; open a bottle and it bubbles out.

Some things that don't dissolve in water dissolve in other liquids — nail-paint dissolves in acetone (nail-paint remover).

keyTerms: Soluble — dissolves in a liquid
Insoluble — does not dissolve
Lustre — natural shine of metals

check.q: Which substance is insoluble in water?
check.why: Chalk powder stays as particles that settle down instead of disappearing into water.

sections.md:
Drop things in a bucket of water: a dry leaf, a wooden block, a cork, a plastic ball **float**; a stone, an iron nail, a coin, a glass marble **sink**. Honey and many oils float or sink in different liquids too.

Floating depends on the material and on shape — a heavy steel ship floats because it is shaped to hold lots of air. You'll learn the full reason in higher classes.

Floating has uses: fishermen use floats on nets; life jackets and buoys keep people and markers afloat.

**Fresh eggs sink in water but float in very salty water** — try it!

check.q: Which will float on water?
check.why: Cork is very light for its size, so it floats; the others sink.

sections.md:
Hold different sheets up to a lit bulb or a window.

- **Transparent**: you can see clearly through them — clear glass, clean water, air, cling film.
- **Translucent**: you can see through, but not clearly — butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper, thin cloth.
- **Opaque**: you can't see through at all — wood, metal, cardboard, a brick wall, your book.

Uses: windows and spectacles need transparent glass; bathroom windows use translucent frosted glass for privacy with light; walls and doors are opaque.

You can make an opaque paper translucent by rubbing a few drops of oil on it.

fig.caption: Light passes fully, partly or not at all.
fig.alt: Light rays passing through glass, butter paper and wood

check.q: Frosted glass in a bathroom window is:
check.why: It lets light in but you can't see clearly through it — translucent.

sections.md:
Now combine all the properties in one investigation. Collect ten objects (with permission): a steel spoon, a wooden ruler, a glass marble, a plastic bottle cap, an eraser, a piece of chalk, an aluminium foil ball, a cotton ball, a coin, a candle.

Test each for every property and record it:

| Object | Material | Lustrous? | Hard/soft | Floats? | Light through? | Soluble in water? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Spoon | Steel | Yes | Hard | Sinks | Opaque | No |
| Ruler | Wood | No | Hard | Floats | Opaque | No |
| Marble | Glass | Shiny-looking | Hard | Sinks | Transparent | No |
| Cap | Plastic | No | Fairly hard | Floats | Opaque/translucent | No |
| Eraser | Rubber | No | Soft | Varies — test | Opaque | No |
| Chalk | Chalk | No | Soft-ish | Sinks | Opaque | No (settles) |
| Foil ball | Aluminium | Yes | Soft (bends) | Floats if loosely crumpled | Opaque | No |
| Cotton | Cotton | No | Soft | Floats at first, then soaks | Translucent (thin) | No |
| Candle | Wax | No | Soft-ish | Floats | Translucent | No |

**What to notice:**

- Every object has **many** properties at once.
- Some results depend on shape — a tightly squeezed foil ball may sink while a loose one floats.
- Some answers are 'it depends' — that is fine in science; write what *you* observed.

**Fair testing:** use the same bucket of water and the same lamp for all objects, so only the object changes.

check.q: A loosely crumpled foil ball floats but a tightly squeezed one sinks. This shows that floating can depend on:
options: Shape and how much air is trapped
check.why: The same material can float or sink depending on its shape and the air trapped inside it.

sections.md:
Engineers and craftspeople pick materials by matching properties to the job.

| Job | Property needed | Good choice |
|---|---|---|
| Cooking pan | Hard, heat-proof, conducts heat | Steel, iron, aluminium |
| Pan handle | Doesn't get hot | Wood, hard plastic |
| Window | Transparent, hard | Glass |
| Raincoat | Waterproof | Plastic, rubberised cloth |
| Summer clothes | Soft, absorbs sweat | Cotton |
| Water storage | Doesn't dissolve or leak | Clay matka, steel, plastic tank |

**Traditional wisdom in materials.** Indian craftspeople have long matched materials to needs: the porous clay **matka** keeps water cool as a little water seeps out and evaporates; **kulhads** are made of clay that returns to the earth; **jute** and **coir** from coconut husk make strong ropes and mats; **bamboo** — light, strong and fast-growing — builds houses and bridges in the North-East; **bell metal** (an alloy) is used for temple bells and vessels in Odisha and Kerala.

check.q: Why is a clay matka good for storing drinking water in summer?
options: Water seeping through its pores evaporates and cools the water
check.why: A little water passes through the porous clay and evaporates from the surface, taking heat away and keeping the water cool.

sections.md:
Every material has a story: where it came from, how much energy it took to make, and where it goes after use.

- **Plastic** is light, cheap, waterproof and does not rust — but most plastic takes hundreds of years to break down. Plastic bags choke drains (making floods worse in cities like Mumbai during the monsoon), harm cattle that eat them, and pollute rivers and seas.
- **Paper and cotton** come from plants and break down naturally, but making them uses trees, water and energy.
- **Metals** like steel and aluminium can be melted and reused again and again — recycling aluminium cans saves most of the energy needed to make new aluminium.
- **Glass** can be cleaned and refilled, or melted and remade.

**The 3 Rs** — in order of importance:

1. **Reduce** — use less: carry a cloth bag, refuse straws.
2. **Reuse** — use again: refill a steel bottle, turn jars into pen stands.
3. **Recycle** — send materials to be remade: separate dry waste (paper, metal, plastic, glass) from wet waste (food peels) so kabadiwalas and recyclers can use it.

India banned many single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022. Choosing materials wisely is not just engineering — it is caring for the Earth.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#f4fff6'/><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 300 130' to='360 300 130' dur='14s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><path d='M300,40 A90,90 0 0 1 378,175' fill='none' stroke='#00b894' stroke-width='14'/><path d='M378,175 A90,90 0 0 1 222,175' fill='none' stroke='#0984e3' stroke-width='14'/><path d='M222,175 A90,90 0 0 1 300,40' fill='none' stroke='#fdcb6e' stroke-width='14'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='18' font-weight='bold' text-anchor='middle'><text x='300' y='125' fill='#2d3436'>3 Rs</text><text x='300' y='150' font-size='13' fill='#636e72'>care for materials</text><text x='440' y='70' fill='#00b894'>Reduce</text><text x='300' y='250' fill='#0984e3'>Reuse</text><text x='150' y='70' fill='#e1a100'>Recycle</text></g></svg>
