check.q: Why do mountain farmers cut terraces into hillsides?
options: To create flat steps for farming and reduce soil being washed away
check.why: Terraces give flat land for crops on steep slopes and slow down rainwater so soil is not eroded.

sections.md:
A **plateau** is an elevated, mostly flat-topped area of land that stands higher than the surrounding area, with one or more steep sides. Think of it as a **table-land**.

The **Deccan Plateau** covers much of peninsular India — parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Its north-western part is made of ancient lava flows that cooled into **black basalt rock**, which weathered into fertile **black soil**, excellent for **cotton**. The **Chota Nagpur Plateau** in Jharkhand is rich in coal, iron and other minerals. Beyond India, the **Tibetan Plateau** is the highest and largest plateau in the world, often called the *Roof of the World*. Africa's East African plateau is famous for its grasslands and wildlife.

**Why plateaus matter**

- They are storehouses of **minerals** — iron ore, coal, manganese, mica, gold (the Kolar fields in Karnataka were famous).
- Rivers flowing off plateau edges make **waterfalls**: Jog Falls on the Sharavathi, Hundru Falls near Ranchi, Dhuandhar on the Narmada.
- Some, like the Deccan lava plateau, have rich soils for farming.
- Cooler hill towns grow on plateau edges.

**Life on plateaus**: people farm cotton, millets (jowar, bajra, ragi), pulses and oilseeds, often depending on rain and **tanks** or wells, because water can be scarce. Many work in **mining** and related industries. Forested plateaus like Chota Nagpur are home to many tribal communities who gather forest produce such as mahua and tendu leaves.

check.q: Which soil, formed from lava rock, makes parts of the Deccan Plateau good for cotton?
check.why: Weathered basalt of the Deccan lava flows forms black soil that holds moisture well, ideal for cotton.

sections.md:
**Plains** are large stretches of flat, low-lying land. Most were formed by **rivers**: as rivers come down from the mountains, they carry fine soil called **silt**. Where the land flattens, the river slows and drops this silt, building up thick layers of fertile **alluvial soil** over thousands of years.

The **Indo-Gangetic plain**, formed by the Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra and their tributaries, is one of the largest and most fertile plains in the world. Where a river meets the sea, it may split into many channels and build a triangle-shaped landform called a **delta** — the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta (home of the Sundarbans) is the world's largest.

**Why plains matter**

- **Fertile soil + water + flat land = farming.** Rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute and pulses grow abundantly.
- Easy to build **roads, railways, canals** and cities.
- That is why plains are the **most densely populated** areas of the world. Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Patna and Kolkata lie in the plains. Ancient civilisations too grew in river plains: the Harappans along the Indus and Sarasvati, Egypt on the Nile, Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates.

**Life in the plains** has challenges too: **floods** in the monsoon (Bihar and Assam often suffer), and crowding, pollution and pressure on groundwater.

check.q: Why are river plains usually crowded with people?
options: They have fertile soil, water and flat land for farming and building
check.why: Flat fertile land and water make farming, transport and cities easy, so populations grow.

sections.h: The sculptors: water, wind and ice
sections.md:
Internal forces raise the land; external forces carve it. Think of them as three sculptors.

**Running water** is the busiest. In the mountains, a young river cuts deep **V-shaped valleys** and gorges. Where it drops over a hard rock edge, it forms a **waterfall**. On the plains it slows down and winds in big loops called **meanders**; in floods it spreads silt over its **floodplain**; at the sea it builds a **delta**.

**Ice** works slowly but powerfully. Glaciers grind the rock beneath them and scoop out wide **U-shaped valleys**. When a glacier melts back, it leaves heaps of rock and soil called **moraines**. The Gangotri glacier has been retreating, and scientists keep careful watch on Himalayan glaciers because millions depend on their meltwater.

**Wind** shapes dry lands. It lifts sand and piles it into **sand dunes**, which slowly march across the Thar Desert; it blasts rocks into mushroom-like shapes. Rows of trees planted as **shelterbelts** help stop dunes spreading onto fields.

**Waves** shape coasts, cutting **cliffs** and sea caves and piling sand into **beaches**.

> Did you know? The Grand Canyon in the USA was carved by the Colorado River over millions of years — patient water can cut through solid rock.

check.q: Sand dunes in the Thar Desert are formed mainly by:
check.why: Wind lifts and drops sand in dry regions, building dunes that slowly move.

sections.md:
Besides the big three, the Earth has many other landforms:

- **Valleys** — low land between hills or mountains, often with a river; e.g. the Kashmir Valley, the Kullu valley.
- **Deserts** — very dry areas with little rain; sandy (the **Thar Desert** in Rajasthan) or cold (Ladakh is a **cold desert**). Desert people like the Raika camel herders and farmers of the Thar use stepwells, *kunds* and *johads* to save every drop of rain.
- **Coasts** — where land meets the sea, with beaches, cliffs and lagoons (like Chilika in Odisha). Fishing, salt-making, ports and tourism are common livelihoods.
- **Islands** — land surrounded by water: the **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** in the Bay of Bengal and **Lakshadweep** (coral islands) in the Arabian Sea.
- **Hills** — lower and more rounded than mountains, like the Nilgiris or the hills of the North-East.

| Landform | Shape | Example in India | Typical livelihoods |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mountain | High, steep, peaked | Himalayas | Herding, terrace farming, tourism |
| Plateau | High, flat-topped | Deccan | Mining, cotton, millets |
| Plain | Low, flat | Indo-Gangetic | Rice, wheat, sugarcane, cities |
| Desert | Dry | Thar | Camel herding, crafts |
| Coast | Edge of sea | Konkan, Coromandel | Fishing, ports |

check.q: Ladakh is described as a:
check.why: Ladakh gets very little rain and is extremely cold, so it is a cold desert.

sections.h: How landforms shape life — and how life shapes landforms
sections.md:
Let us return to our three friends. Tenzin's family wears thick wool, eats barley (*tsampa*) and keeps yaks because the high, cold mountains offer short summers and thin grass. Kavya's family grows cotton in black soil and her uncle works in a granite quarry. Arjun's family grows two crops a year on the fertile plain but worries when the river floods.

Landforms affect:

- **Food** — rice in wet plains, millets on dry plateaus, barley in cold mountains.
- **Clothing and housing** — wool and stone in the hills; light cotton and mud or brick in the plains; flat roofs in dry areas, sloping ones where it snows or rains heavily.
- **Occupations** — herding, farming, mining, fishing, tourism.
- **Festivals and culture** — harvest festivals in plains, mountain deities and sacred peaks, boat races on Kerala's backwaters.

But humans shape landforms too — sometimes harmfully. Cutting forests on slopes causes **landslides**; too much mining scars plateaus; building on river floodplains worsens floods; heavy construction in fragile mountain towns like Joshimath has raised concern. Respecting landforms — planting trees, harvesting rainwater, building wisely — keeps people safe.

> Did you know? Many Indian communities treat mountains, rivers and groves as sacred, which has helped protect them — like the sacred groves (*devrai*, *kavu*) of the Western Ghats.

check.q: Which human activity most directly increases landslides in mountain areas?
check.why: Tree roots hold soil; removing them leaves slopes loose and likely to slide in heavy rain.

parts.md:
When their teacher started a pen-pal project, Arjun from Bihar was paired with Tenzin from Ladakh. Arjun wrote first: *"Our fields are so flat my kite string can run forever. In July the river comes up to our road, and we wait on the roof of the school until it goes down."*

Tenzin replied a month later — the mail truck could not cross the pass for two weeks because of snow. *"I have never seen a flat field as big as you describe! Our fields are tiny steps on the mountain. In winter our stream freezes so hard my little sister slides on it. We melt ice for water."*

Then Kavya joined from Telangana. *"I live on a giant table!"* she wrote. *"The Deccan Plateau is high but flat on top. My grandmother's cotton fields are black, sticky soil after rain. We get less rain than Arjun, so our village keeps an old tank full for the dry months. And near my school there is a waterfall where the plateau suddenly ends."*

At the end of the year the three made a shared poster: three drawings, one country, and the title — *The land decides much, but people decide the rest.*

summary: Landforms are natural features of the Earth's surface shaped by internal forces and by erosion and deposition.
The three main landforms are mountains, plateaus and plains.
Mountains are high with steep slopes; the Himalayas are the youngest and highest range.
Mountains give rivers (via glaciers), block cold winds, trap monsoon rain and support forests and tourism.
Mountain life involves terrace farming, herding, seasonal movement and adapted housing.
Plateaus are elevated flat-topped table-lands; the Deccan and Chota Nagpur are examples.
Plateaus are rich in minerals and have waterfalls; the Deccan's black soil suits cotton.
Plains are flat low lands built by river silt; the Indo-Gangetic plain is very fertile.
Plains are densely populated and were cradles of early civilisations, but face floods.
Rivers carve V-valleys, waterfalls, meanders and deltas; glaciers make U-valleys and moraines; wind builds dunes.
Other landforms include valleys, deserts (hot Thar, cold Ladakh), coasts and islands.
Landforms shape food, clothes, houses, jobs and culture; humans in turn reshape landforms, sometimes harmfully.

glossary.d: Wearing away of land by water, wind or ice.
Laying down of eroded material.
Raised flat-topped land.
A large loop in a river on flat land.
Rock and soil left behind by a glacier.
Dry, cold area with little rain, like Ladakh.

rd-school-c6-social-a.ch04-timeline-sour.title: Timeline and Sources of History
rd-school-c6-social-a.ch04-timeline-sour.subtitle: How we count the centuries, and how historians become detectives of the past

sections.md:
In a rock shelter at **Bhimbetka**, near Bhopal, there are paintings of bison, deer, hunters and dancers in red and white. Some may be over 10,000 years old. No one left a note saying who painted them or when. So how can we know anything about them?

That is the work of the **historian** — a detective of the past. Like any detective, a historian needs two things:

1. a way to **place events in time** — to know what happened before what, and how long ago; and
2. **evidence**, or **sources**, that tell us what happened.

This chapter is about both: the **timeline** and the **sources of history**. We will also take a quick journey through the very long story of early humans — the longest chapter of the human past.

sections.h: Measuring time: years, decades, centuries, millennia
sections.md:
We group years into bigger units, just as we group paise into rupees:

| Unit | Length |
|---|---|
| Decade | 10 years |
| Century | 100 years |
| Millennium (plural millennia) | 1,000 years |

Centuries are counted in a slightly tricky way. The **1st century CE** is years 1 to 100; the **2nd century** is 101 to 200. So the **20th century** is 1901–2000 and we now live in the **21st century** (2001–2100). Quick rule: for a year like 1857, drop the last two digits and add one → 18 + 1 = **19th century**. (For a year ending in 00, such as 1900, it is the 19th century — the last year of that century.)

**Decades** are often named by their first year: 'the 1990s' means 1990–1999.

> Did you know? The year 2000 belonged to the 20th century, not the 21st — many people celebrated the new millennium a year early!

check.q: In which century is the year 1757?
check.why: Drop the last two digits (17) and add one: the 18th century, which runs from 1701 to 1800.

sections.h: BCE and CE — the dividing line
sections.md:
Most of the world today uses a calendar called the **Gregorian calendar**. Its years are counted from a traditional date for the birth of Jesus Christ.

- Years after this point are labelled **CE** (*Common Era*); older books write **AD** (*Anno Domini*, Latin for 'in the year of the Lord').
- Years before it are labelled **BCE** (*Before Common Era*); older books write **BC** ('Before Christ').

Important: there is **no year 0**. The year before 1 CE is 1 BCE.

**Counting BCE is backwards.** In BCE, bigger numbers are *older*. 2500 BCE is earlier than 500 BCE. It is like a countdown to 1 CE. Likewise the '5th century BCE' (500–401 BCE) comes *before* the '4th century BCE'.

On a **timeline**, we draw a line with BCE dates on the left, getting smaller towards the middle, then CE dates increasing to the right.

**How long ago?**

- Between two CE dates: subtract. From 1947 CE to 2025 CE = 2025 − 1947 = 78 years.
- Between two BCE dates: subtract the smaller from the larger. 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE = 700 years.
- From a BCE date to a CE date: **add** them, then subtract 1 (because there is no year 0). From 300 BCE to 300 CE = 300 + 300 − 1 = **599 years**. (For rough estimates historians often just add.)

India has many other traditional calendars too, such as the **Vikram Samvat** (which begins in 57 BCE) and the **Shaka Samvat** (beginning in 78 CE), which is the basis of India's official national calendar. Other communities use the Hijri calendar, Kollam era in Kerala, or the Bengali calendar — each counting from a different starting point.

check.q: Which date is the oldest?
check.why: In BCE, larger numbers are further back in time, so 1200 BCE is the oldest.

sections.h: The scale of time: if Earth's story were one day
sections.md:
Dates in history books go back a few thousand years. But the Earth is about **4.5 billion** (450 crore) years old. How do we picture such vast time?

Imagine squeezing the whole history of the Earth into **one day of 24 hours**, starting at midnight:

- Each hour then stands for about 19 crore years.
- The first simple life appears in the early morning hours.
- Dinosaurs arrive late in the evening, around 10:45 pm, and vanish around 11:40 pm.
- *Homo sapiens* — our species, about 3,00,000 years old — appears only in the **last 6 seconds** before midnight. (3,00,000 ÷ 4,50,00,00,000 × 86,400 seconds ≈ 5.8 seconds.)
- All of written history, about 5,000 years, fits into the last **tenth of a second**.

So human history is a tiny sliver of Earth's story, and recorded history is a sliver of human history. That is why historians work alongside scientists such as **geologists** (who study rocks) and **palaeontologists** (who study fossils) for the deep past.

check.q: If Earth's history were a single day, written history would take about:
check.why: About 5,000 years out of 4.5 billion is a tiny fraction — roughly a tenth of a second in a 24-hour day.

sections.md:
A **source** is anything that gives us information about the past. Historians group them like this:

**1. Archaeological sources** — physical remains dug up or found:
- **Tools, pottery, beads, bones, seeds** — e.g. burnt grains reveal what people ate.
- **Buildings and cities** — the drains and streets of Harappan cities; temples; stupas.
- **Paintings** — like those at Bhimbetka.

An **archaeologist** carefully excavates (digs) sites layer by layer. Deeper layers are generally older — this idea is called **stratigraphy**. Scientific methods such as **carbon dating** help estimate the age of things that were once alive, such as wood, bone or grain.

**2. Inscriptions** — writing carved on hard surfaces like stone, metal or rock. The **edicts of Emperor Ashoka** (3rd century BCE), carved on rocks and pillars, are among the oldest deciphered inscriptions in India. Copper-plate grants recorded gifts of land.

**3. Coins** — tell us about kings, trade, metals, symbols and beliefs. Punch-marked silver coins are among India's earliest.

**4. Literary sources** — texts and manuscripts: religious texts (the Vedas, Buddhist and Jain texts), epics, poetry (like Sangam poems in Tamil), plays, scientific works and accounts of travellers (like the Greek Megasthenes or the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang). Many were written on **palm leaves** or **birch bark** and copied by hand over centuries.

**5. Oral traditions** — songs, stories, legends and genealogies passed by word of mouth. The Vedas were preserved orally with amazing accuracy for many centuries before being written down.

Good historians **compare** sources. A king's inscription may boast; a traveller may misunderstand; an object cannot lie but needs interpretation. When several sources agree, we can be more confident.

head: Type of source
Example
What it can tell us
fig.caption: Different sources answer different questions.

check.q: Ashoka's edicts carved on rocks and pillars are an example of which source?
check.why: Writing carved on hard surfaces like rock or pillars is called an inscription.

sections.md:
No single person can read every kind of clue. History is built by a team of specialists:

| Specialist | Studies | Example of their work |
|---|---|---|
| **Archaeologist** | Material remains, excavation | Digging at Dholavira or Rakhigarhi |
| **Epigraphist** | Inscriptions | James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script of Ashoka's edicts in 1837 |
| **Numismatist** | Coins | Tracing trade routes through Roman coins found in South India |
| **Palaeontologist** | Fossils of plants and animals | Dinosaur fossils of Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh |
| **Anthropologist** | Human societies and cultures | Studying how forest communities live today |
| **Geneticist** | DNA | Ancient DNA from a Rakhigarhi skeleton |
| **Linguist** | Languages and their histories | How words travel between languages |

Sometimes a single find needs all of them. A skeleton dug up by archaeologists might be dated by scientists, its DNA read by geneticists, and the pots beside it compared with pots from other sites.

> Did you know? The Harappan script on seals has still **not been deciphered**. Hundreds of scholars have tried. Until someone succeeds, the Harappans' own words remain a mystery.

check.q: A scholar who studies old coins is called a:
check.why: Numismatics is the study of coins, so the specialist is a numismatist.

sections.h: The very long story of early humans
sections.md:
The human story is far longer than written history.

- Our species, ***Homo sapiens***, first appeared in **Africa** around **3,00,000 years ago**, according to fossil evidence.
- Groups of humans spread out of Africa; scientists' estimates for when modern humans reached the Indian subcontinent vary, but many suggest roughly 50,000–70,000 years ago or earlier. (Stone tools in India are even older, made by earlier human species.)
- For most of this time humans were **hunter-gatherers**: they hunted animals, fished, and gathered fruits, roots, seeds and honey. They moved from place to place following food and water, and lived in rock shelters or temporary huts.
- They made **stone tools** — hand-axes, choppers, scrapers, later tiny sharp **microliths** set in handles to make arrows and sickles. Places like **Hunsgi** (Karnataka) and **Attirampakkam** (Tamil Nadu) give evidence of very early tools.
- They learnt to control **fire** — for warmth, cooking, light and scaring away animals.
- They painted on rock walls — Bhimbetka is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The period before writing is called **prehistory**. Because there are no written records, archaeological sources are our main clues for it.

check.q: Why are archaeological sources our main evidence for prehistory?
options: There was no writing in that period
check.why: Prehistory is by definition the time before writing, so only physical remains survive as evidence.

sections.md:
Around **10,000–12,000 years ago**, the world's climate grew warmer after the last Ice Age. In several parts of the world, people began to **domesticate** plants and animals — to grow crops and raise herds deliberately.

In the Indian subcontinent, one of the best-known early farming sites is **Mehrgarh**, at the foot of the Bolan Pass in present-day Balochistan (Pakistan). By around **7000 BCE**, people there grew **barley and wheat**, kept **cattle, sheep and goats**, built mud-brick houses with several rooms, and buried their dead with goods. Later evidence there shows bead-making and even early tooth drilling!

Farming changed everything:

- People **settled** in one place → villages.
- Food could be stored → **surplus**, more people, specialised crafts (potters, weavers, bead-makers).
- New tools: grinding stones, sickles, pots for storage and cooking.
- Eventually, villages grew into towns and cities — leading to the Harappan civilisation.

Hunting-gathering did not vanish overnight; many communities combined it with farming and herding, and forest communities kept such ways of life for a long time.

> Did you know? A domesticated plant or animal is one that humans have selected and cared for over many generations, so it becomes different from its wild relatives — like wheat grains that no longer fall off the stalk on their own.

check.q: Which change came directly with farming?
options: People began living in settled villages
Writing was invented the same year
check.why: Growing crops tied people to their fields, so they settled in permanent villages.

check.q: A historian finds that a king's inscription claims a great victory, but another source says he lost. What should she do?
options: Believe the inscription because it is carved in stone
Compare more sources and consider why each might be biased
check.why: Historians cross-check sources and think about each author's purpose before drawing conclusions.

parts.md:
During the Diwali cleaning, Meher found a rusted tin trunk under her grandmother's bed. Inside: a black-and-white photo of a young man in a railway uniform, a 1962 ration card, a postcard with a Shimla postmark, a silver coin with a king's head dated 1919, and a folded wedding card printed in Gujarati.

"Who is this?" she asked, holding the photo. Ba smiled. "Your great-grandfather. He was a station master on the line to Shimla."

Meher spread everything on the floor and drew a line on chart paper. The coin went first — 1919, the 20th century. The wedding card said 1948. The ration card, 1962. Ba remembered that the photo was taken 'a year after the wedding', so 1949. The postcard's stamp was smudged; Meher placed it with a question mark, the way real historians do.

By evening she had a family timeline built from objects, writing and her grandmother's memories — archaeological, written and oral sources, all in one tin trunk. "So history," she announced, "is just very careful remembering."

workedExamples.q: How many years passed between the founding of a city in 2600 BCE and its decline in 1900 BCE?
steps: Subtract the smaller from the larger: 2600 − 1900.

steps: One date BCE, one CE: add them.
Subtract 1 because there is no year 0.

steps: BCE dates come first, larger number older: 326 BCE, then 57 BCE.
Then CE in increasing order: 1 CE, 78 CE.

summary: Historians place events in time and use evidence (sources) to understand the past.
Decade = 10 years, century = 100, millennium = 1,000.
The 21st century runs from 2001 to 2100.
CE years count forward; BCE years count backward — bigger BCE number means older.
There is no year 0; 1 BCE is followed by 1 CE.
India also uses calendars like Vikram Samvat (from 57 BCE) and Shaka Samvat (from 78 CE).
Earth is about 4.5 billion years old; humans are a tiny recent part of its story.
Sources include archaeological remains, inscriptions, coins, literary texts and oral traditions.
Archaeologists excavate layer by layer; carbon dating helps date once-living material.
Epigraphists, numismatists, palaeontologists, geneticists and linguists help historians.
Homo sapiens appeared in Africa about 3,00,000 years ago; hunter-gatherers used stone tools and fire.
Farming began around 10,000–12,000 years ago; Mehrgarh shows farming by about 7000 BCE.
Historians compare sources and revise conclusions when new evidence appears.

Careful digging of a site.

Time before writing.

check.why: The Himalayas and associated ranges separate the subcontinent from the rest of Asia in the north.

sections.h: Names from within: Jambudvipa and Bharata
sections.md:
**Jambudvipa.** Some of the oldest Indian texts — Hindu, Buddhist and Jain — describe the world as a set of island-continents (*dvipas*). The one where humans live is **Jambudvipa**, 'the island of the *jambu* tree' — the jamun or Indian blackberry tree, familiar to every child who has eaten its purple fruit in summer. Emperor **Ashoka**, in one of his inscriptions in the 3rd century BCE, used the word *Jambudipa* for the lands he ruled. Over time, Jambudvipa came to refer especially to the Indian subcontinent.

**Bharata.** The **Rig Veda**, one of the world's oldest texts, mentions the **Bharatas**, a prominent clan or people who lived in the north-west of the subcontinent. Many scholars think the name of the land may be linked to them. Later texts connect the name to a legendary king named **Bharata**.

**Bharatavarsha** ('the land of the Bharatas') appears in the **Mahabharata** and the **Puranas**. A well-known verse in the *Vishnu Purana* describes it roughly as the land lying north of the ocean and south of the snowy mountains, where the descendants of Bharata dwell. So the name described not one kingdom, but the whole land between the Himalayas and the sea.

The name **Bharatavarsha** also appears in the **Hathigumpha inscription** of **King Kharavela** of Kalinga (in present-day Odisha), from around the 1st century BCE.

> Did you know? In most Indian languages today — Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and more — the country is called *Bharat* or a close form of it.

check.q: The name 'Jambudvipa' refers to which tree?
check.why: Jambudvipa means the island of the jambu tree, the jamun or Indian blackberry.

sections.h: Names for regions inside the land
sections.md:
Inside this large land, people also had names for its **regions**. These names show how they understood the geography around them.

- **Aryavarta** — in some ancient Sanskrit texts, the land of the north between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains. Different texts drew its limits differently.
- **Dakshinapatha** — literally 'the southern route'; the trade road and the lands south of the Vindhyas. The word lives on in **Deccan**.
- **Tamilakam** — the Tamil-speaking land of the south in Sangam literature, stretching, as the poets put it, from Venkatam (the hills near Tirupati) to Kumari (the southern tip).
- **Kamarupa** — the ancient kingdom in present-day Assam, mentioned in inscriptions and by the traveller Xuanzang.
- **Kalinga**, **Magadha**, **Gandhara**, **Kashi**, **Vanga** and others — names of old kingdoms and regions, many still used for places or cultures today (Vanga → Bengal).

These regional names did not compete with the larger ideas of Jambudvipa or Bharatavarsha. A person could belong to Kalinga *and* to Bharatavarsha at the same time — just as today someone is an Odia, an Indian, and a citizen of the world all at once.

> Did you know? Sangam poems describe Tamil kings sending gifts and receiving traders from far lands, and mention the Himalayas in the north — showing that southern poets too imagined the whole land from mountain to sea.

check.q: The word 'Deccan' comes from which old regional name?
check.why: Dakshinapatha meant the southern route or southern land; Deccan comes from the same root 'dakshina' (south).

sections.h: Names from outside: Sindhu, Hindu, Indoi, India
sections.md:
Neighbours often name a land after the first big feature they meet. For people coming from the north-west, that feature was the great river **Sindhu** — the **Indus**.

- The **ancient Persians** (of the Achaemenid Empire, around the 6th century BCE) pronounced the 's' sound at the start of 'Sindhu' as 'h'. So *Sindhu* became **Hindu**, used for the land and people near and beyond the river. Inscriptions of the Persian king **Darius I** name a province called *Hidush* (roughly the Indus region).
- The **ancient Greeks** learnt the word from the Persians. They dropped the 'h' and called the river *Indos* and the people **Indoi**. From there came **India**, through Latin and later European languages. **Megasthenes**, the Greek envoy who stayed at the court of Chandragupta Maurya around 300 BCE, wrote a book called *Indika* about the land.
- The **Chinese** used names like *Shendu* and later **Yintu**. The famous Buddhist pilgrim **Xuanzang**, who travelled through India in the 7th century CE and studied at Nalanda, used *Yintu* and explained its meaning in his own way.
- Later, Persian and Arabic writers used **Hindustan** ('land of the Hind'), especially for northern India, and *al-Hind*.

Notice: in these early uses, words like 'Hindu' were **geographical** — they named a land and its people, not a particular religion. The religious meaning came much later.

sections.md:
Foreign visitors left some of the most vivid descriptions of the land they named.

**Megasthenes (around 300 BCE).** Sent as an envoy by the Greek ruler Seleucus to the Mauryan court at **Pataliputra** (near today's Patna), he described a huge, well-guarded city with wooden walls, many gates and towers. His *Indika* is lost; we know parts of it only because later Greek and Roman writers quoted it. So historians read it carefully — some details may be exaggerated or misunderstood.

**Xuanzang (7th century CE).** A Chinese Buddhist monk who walked across Central Asia to India to collect Buddhist texts. He spent years at **Nalanda**, the great centre of learning, and travelled widely before returning to China with hundreds of manuscripts. His record describes kingdoms, monasteries, customs and climate, and tells us about the court of King Harsha.

**Al-Biruni (11th century CE).** A scholar from Central Asia who learnt Sanskrit and wrote a long book about Indian sciences, beliefs and customs, using the name *al-Hind*.

Why do these accounts matter? They are **outside views**: they notice things locals took for granted, but they can also misread what they did not understand. Historians compare them with Indian texts and inscriptions — exactly the method you learnt in the previous chapter.

sections.h: From many names to one Constitution
sections.md:
By the time of British rule, *India* was the common name in English, while *Bharat*, *Hindustan* and regional names lived on in Indian languages. During the freedom struggle, slogans and songs used all of them — *Bharat Mata*, *Hindustan*, *India*.

When the **Constituent Assembly** wrote the Constitution (adopted on **26 November 1949**, in force from **26 January 1950**), members debated what to call the new republic. Some preferred *Bharat* alone, others suggested *Bharatvarsha* or *Hindustan*. The final wording, *"India, that is Bharat"*, kept both: the international name and the ancient name from within. (26 November is now celebrated as **Constitution Day**.)

Today:

- In English, we usually say *India*; in Hindi, *Bharat*. Our passports and currency notes carry both — *Bharat* in Devanagari and *India* in English.
- Government bodies use both: *Bharatiya Rail* / Indian Railways; *Bharatiya Reserve Bank* / Reserve Bank of India.

The many names are not in competition. Together they record a long history: a land that its own people saw as one sacred geography from the mountains to the sea, and that the world came to know through its great river.

check.q: When did the Constitution with the words 'India, that is Bharat' come into force?
check.why: It was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950, our Republic Day.

sections.md:
Studying names is a kind of history detective work. From this chapter we learn:

1. **The idea of a single land is very old.** Long before modern maps, Indian texts imagined Bharatavarsha or Jambudvipa as one land, even with many kings.
2. **Rivers and mountains shaped identity.** The Sindhu gave the world 'India'; the Himalayas and the oceans defined the land's edges.
3. **India was always connected.** Persians, Greeks, Chinese, Arabs knew of India and wrote about it because of trade and travel.
4. **Words change as they travel** — Sindhu → Hindu → Indos → India.
5. **Sources matter.** Our knowledge comes from texts (Vedas, Puranas, Sangam poems), inscriptions (Ashoka, Kharavela, Darius), and travellers' accounts (Megasthenes, Xuanzang).

> Think about it: What is your city or village called in different languages? Does it have an old name? Ask an elder — you may find your own 'layers of names'.

check.q: Which of these is an INSIDE (Indian) source that uses the term Bharatavarsha?
check.why: King Kharavela of Kalinga's Hathigumpha inscription is an Indian source that mentions Bharatavarsha.

story.title: Five Names at the Railway Station

parts.md:
Riya's train was late at Varanasi Junction, so she started reading every sign on the platform. The station board said *Varanasi* in Hindi, English and Urdu. A tea-seller called it *Banaras*. A pilgrim beside her said softly, "Kashi." Her father, a history teacher, laughed. "Three names for one city — and each from a different layer of time."

"Like our country," said Riya, pointing at her passport, which said *Bharat Ganarajya* on top and *Republic of India* below.

Her father took out his notebook and drew an arrow: *Sindhu → Hindu → Indos → India*. "The river named the land for the world," he said. Then he wrote *Jambudvipa* and *Bharatavarsha* above it. "And these are what the land called itself."

When the train finally came, Riya wrote in her diary: *A name is like a ticket — it tells you where something has travelled.*

rd-school-c6-social-a.ch06-beginnings-ci.title: The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation
rd-school-c6-social-a.ch06-beginnings-ci.subtitle: Planned cities, covered drains, sea trade and a script still unread — the Harappan world

check.q: Which of these is NOT usually a feature of a civilisation?
options: Living only by hunting and moving constantly
check.why: Civilisations are marked by settled cities and surplus food, not a fully nomadic hunting life.

sections.md:
For centuries, local people knew the mounds near Harappa simply as old ruins; in the 19th century, railway builders even carried away bricks from them to lay under railway tracks!

- In **1921**, **Daya Ram Sahni** of the Archaeological Survey of India began excavations at **Harappa**.
- In **1922**, **R. D. Banerji** began digging at **Mohenjo-daro**, over 600 km away, and found similar seals and objects.
- In **1924**, **Sir John Marshall**, Director-General of the Survey, announced to the world that a new, very ancient civilisation had been found.

After 1947, when Harappa and Mohenjo-daro went to Pakistan, Indian archaeologists searched hard within India and found many more sites — **Lothal** and **Dholavira** in Gujarat, **Kalibangan** in Rajasthan, **Rakhigarhi** in Haryana. Digging still continues, and new finds keep changing our picture.

> Did you know? 'Mohenjo-daro' is usually said to mean 'mound of the dead' in Sindhi — a name given much later by local people, not by the Harappans themselves. We do not know what the Harappans called their own cities.

check.q: Who began excavations at Harappa in 1921?
check.why: Daya Ram Sahni led the first excavations at Harappa in 1921; Banerji dug at Mohenjo-daro in 1922.

sections.md:
The **mature Harappan phase** lasted roughly from **2600 BCE to 1900 BCE**, though earlier and later phases stretch the story from about 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE.

More than **1,500 sites** have been found, spread over present-day **Pakistan, north-western India** and parts of **Afghanistan**. Important cities include:

| Site | Where today | Famous for |
|---|---|---|
| Harappa | Punjab, Pakistan | First site excavated (1921) |
| Mohenjo-daro | Sindh, Pakistan | Great Bath, granary-like building |
| Dholavira | Kutch, Gujarat | Reservoirs, big signboard; UNESCO site |
| Lothal | Gujarat | Dockyard-like basin, bead factory |
| Kalibangan | Rajasthan | Ploughed field, fire altars |
| Rakhigarhi | Haryana | One of the largest Harappan sites |
| Ganweriwala | Punjab, Pakistan | Large site on Ghaggar-Hakra plain |

Many sites lie along the dry bed of the **Ghaggar-Hakra**, which suggests that this river, often linked with the Sarasvati of the Rig Veda, was once a major river.

sections.md:
Harappan cities were remarkably well planned:

- **Grid streets.** Main streets ran roughly north–south and east–west, crossing at right angles and dividing the city into blocks.
- **Two parts.** Many cities had a raised western part (often called the *citadel*) with large buildings, and a larger lower town where most people lived. Dholavira had three parts — citadel, middle town and lower town — enclosed by walls.
- **Standard bricks.** Bricks were made in a fixed ratio of about **1 : 2 : 4** (thickness : width : length), whether in Harappa or in Gujarat hundreds of kilometres away. This suggests shared rules and skills.
- **Houses** were often one or two storeys, built around a courtyard, with rooms, a well and a bathroom. Doors usually opened onto side lanes rather than main streets.
- **Drainage.** Bathrooms drained into covered brick drains along the streets, with inspection holes for cleaning. Few ancient cities anywhere had such systems.

**The Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro is a large rectangular tank (about 12 m × 7 m and 2.4 m deep), made watertight with fitted bricks and a layer of bitumen (natural tar), with steps at both ends. Scholars think it was used for special ritual bathing.

> Did you know? Mohenjo-daro may have had hundreds of wells.

check.q: Why did Dholavira's people build large reservoirs?
options: To store scarce rainwater for dry months
check.why: Kutch gets little rain, so storing every monsoon's water was essential for survival.

sections.md:
City people depended on farmers in surrounding villages. Harappans grew **wheat, barley, pulses (lentils, peas), sesame, mustard** and, in some areas, **millets** and **rice**. They were among the earliest people in the world to grow **cotton**. At **Kalibangan**, archaeologists found a **ploughed field** with criss-cross furrows — a pattern still used by some farmers in Rajasthan! Animals included cattle, sheep, goats, buffaloes and pigs.

**Crafts** were highly skilled:

- **Beads** of carnelian (a red stone), lapis lazuli, steatite and gold; the long carnelian beads were drilled with special drills — a very difficult job.
- **Pottery** — red pots painted with black designs.
- **Metal work** in copper and bronze — tools, vessels, mirrors and the famous small bronze statuette of a woman often called the **'Dancing Girl'** from Mohenjo-daro.
- **Shell bangles** and ornaments, especially from coastal Gujarat.
- **Weights** — cubes of chert in a standard system (in ratios like 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…), used across the whole region for fair trade.

check.q: What does the ploughed field at Kalibangan show?
options: Harappans used ploughs and planned furrows
check.why: Criss-cross furrows reveal that Harappan farmers ploughed fields systematically.

sections.h: Daily life in a Harappan town
sections.md:
What might an ordinary day have looked like? From objects found in houses, archaeologists can piece together a picture.

- **Clothes and ornaments.** Spindle whorls (weights used for spinning thread) show that people spun cotton and wool. Men and women wore ornaments — necklaces, bangles, ear-rings, girdles of beads. Many women seem to have worn many bangles, as figurines show.
- **Food.** Grinding stones, storage jars and cooking pots tell of breads and porridges of wheat and barley, pulses, fruits like dates, milk products, fish and meat.
- **Games and toys.** Children played with clay toy carts with moving wheels, whistles shaped like birds, tops, marbles, and animals whose heads nod on a string. Dice and gaming boards suggest board games for adults.
- **Transport.** Clay models of **bullock carts** look much like carts still used in Indian villages today. Boats carried goods along rivers and the coast.
- **Cleanliness.** Bathing platforms in houses and the drainage system show great care for hygiene.

We should remember that most Harappans were not city-dwellers but **villagers** — farmers and herders living in small settlements around the cities.

check.q: Spindle whorls found in Harappan houses tell us that people:
check.why: Spindle whorls are weights used when spinning fibre into thread, showing cloth-making at home.

sections.md:
Harappans traded raw materials and goods within the subcontinent and far beyond:

- Copper from Rajasthan (Khetri area), shells from Gujarat, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, gold possibly from Karnataka.
- **Overseas trade** with **Mesopotamia** (in today's Iraq) and the Gulf region (Dilmun, today's Bahrain; Magan, today's Oman). Mesopotamian records mention a land called **Meluhha**, which many historians identify with the Harappan region. Harappan seals and carnelian beads have been found in Mesopotamia.

At **Lothal**, a large brick basin connected to a river channel has been interpreted by many archaeologists as a **dockyard** for boats; others think it may have been a water reservoir — a good example of historians debating evidence.

sections.h: Seals, an unread script — and who ruled?
sections.md:
Thousands of small square **seals** made of **steatite** (soapstone) have been found. They usually show an animal — often a one-horned animal (sometimes called a 'unicorn'), a bull, elephant, tiger or rhinoceros — along with a short line of **signs**. Seals may have been pressed onto clay to mark goods or show ownership or authority.

The **Harappan script** has about 400 signs and was probably written mostly from right to left. Inscriptions are very short — usually about five signs — and there is no bilingual inscription (like Egypt's Rosetta Stone) to help. So the script has **not yet been deciphered**.

**Who governed?** Unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia, no grand palaces, royal tombs or statues of kings have been clearly identified. Yet standard bricks, weights and city plans point to strong organisation. Historians suggest councils of elders, merchants or priests may have managed cities; perhaps each city had its own rulers. We simply do not know for sure.

**Beliefs.** Without readable texts, we guess from objects: clay figurines, fire altars (Kalibangan, Lothal), the Great Bath, and a seal showing a figure seated in a yoga-like posture surrounded by animals. Some practices — reverence for trees like the peepal, ritual bathing — seem to continue in later Indian culture, but historians are careful in interpreting them.

check.q: Why has the Harappan script not been deciphered?
options: Inscriptions are very short and no bilingual text has been found
It is the same as English
check.why: Short texts and the lack of a bilingual key, like the Rosetta Stone, make decipherment extremely hard.

sections.md:
Around **1900 BCE**, the great cities began to decline. Drains were no longer maintained, buildings were poorly made, the script and seals faded out, and many people moved to smaller villages, especially eastward and southward.

Why? There is no single answer. Historians and scientists suggest a combination of causes:

- **Climate change** — evidence suggests weaker monsoons and drier conditions for a long period.
- **Drying up of the Sarasvati / Ghaggar-Hakra** as rivers shifted course.
- **Floods** and river changes in the Indus region.
- Decline in **trade** with Mesopotamia.

An older idea of a sudden 'invasion' is not supported by the archaeological evidence.

Importantly, **people did not vanish**. Village life continued, and many Harappan skills and practices — standard weights, bead-making, farming methods such as criss-cross ploughing, shell bangles, bullock carts of similar design, care for water — fed into later Indian life. That is why the chapter is called *the beginnings* of Indian civilisation.

check.q: Which best describes current thinking on the decline of Harappan cities?
options: Several causes like climate change and rivers drying, over a long period
A single earthquake in one day
check.why: Evidence points to gradual decline from several factors, especially climate and river changes, rather than one event.

parts.md:
*(An imagined story based on archaeological evidence.)* In the bead workshop at Lothal, a boy named Sindhu watched his mother hold a long red carnelian bead against a tiny stone drill. She had been drilling it for three days. "One slip," she said, "and three days are gone." When it was done, it gleamed like a drop of sunset.

The merchant who bought it pressed his steatite seal — a one-horned animal and five signs — onto a lump of clay tied to the bundle.

Weeks later the bundle sailed out with the tide, past the dockyard basin, west across the Arabian Sea. In a city on the far river Euphrates, a scribe wrote on a clay tablet that goods had come from *Meluhha*.

Four thousand years later, an archaeologist in Iraq brushed the dust off a long red bead and smiled. She knew exactly where such beads were made. The seal's five signs, though, she still could not read.

summary: A civilisation has cities, administration, specialised crafts, trade, writing and a food surplus.
Harappa was excavated in 1921 (Daya Ram Sahni), Mohenjo-daro in 1922 (R. D. Banerji); Marshall announced the find in 1924.
The Harappan (Indus / Indus-Sarasvati) civilisation's mature phase lasted c. 2600–1900 BCE.
It covered the largest area among early civilisations, with over 1,500 sites.
Key sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi.
Cities had grid streets, citadels, standard 1:2:4 bricks, houses with bathrooms, and covered drains.
The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro was a watertight ritual tank.
Dholavira's dams and reservoirs show advanced water management; it is a UNESCO site.
Harappans grew wheat, barley, pulses, cotton; Kalibangan has a ploughed field.
Crafts: carnelian beads, pottery, bronze (Dancing Girl), shell work, standard weights.
Toys, ornaments, spindle whorls and cart models reveal daily life.
Trade reached Mesopotamia ('Meluhha'); Lothal had a dock-like basin.
Steatite seals carry an undeciphered script of about 400 signs; how cities were ruled is uncertain.
Cities declined after c. 1900 BCE due to several causes, but village life and many traditions continued.

rd-school-c6-social-a.ch07-cultural-root.title: India's Cultural Roots
rd-school-c6-social-a.ch07-cultural-root.subtitle: The Vedas, the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira and the folk and tribal wisdom that grew into one great banyan

items.what: Rig Veda hymns composed in the Sapta Sindhu region
Other Vedas, Brahmanas; early Upanishads
Lives of the Buddha and Mahavira
Ashoka supports the spread of Buddhism
Folk and tribal traditions grow alongside, passed on orally

fig.caption: An approximate sequence; exact dates are debated by scholars.

sections.md:
The word **Veda** comes from the Sanskrit root *vid*, 'to know'. The Vedas are a vast collection of hymns, prayers and ritual knowledge composed in an early form of Sanskrit. There are **four Vedas**:

| Veda | Main content |
|---|---|
| **Rig Veda** | Over 1,000 hymns (*suktas*) to deities like Agni (fire), Indra, Varuna, Surya, Ushas (dawn) |
| **Sama Veda** | Melodies (*samans*) for singing hymns; important for the history of Indian music |
| **Yajur Veda** | Formulas and instructions for rituals (*yajnas*) |
| **Atharva Veda** | Hymns for daily life, healing, protection and well-being |

The **Rig Veda** is the oldest; many scholars place its composition broadly in the 2nd millennium BCE, though dates are debated. It was composed mainly in the region of the **Sapta Sindhu** ('land of seven rivers') in north-western India.

**Oral tradition.** For many centuries the Vedas were not written down. They were memorised and passed from teacher to student with astonishing precision using special recitation methods — reciting words forwards, in pairs, and in complex patterns so that a single mistake would be noticed. **UNESCO** has recognised Vedic chanting as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage.

**Ideas in the Vedas.**

- **Rita** — a cosmic order that keeps the universe, seasons and life in balance; this idea later grew into **dharma** (duty, right conduct).
- Respect for **nature** — fire, water, rivers, dawn, earth were honoured.
- Questions about creation: one famous hymn, the *Nasadiya Sukta*, wonders how the universe began and ends by suggesting that perhaps even the highest one does not know — a remarkable spirit of questioning.
- Assemblies called **sabha** and **samiti** where people discussed matters.
- Women composers: some hymns are credited to women seers such as **Lopamudra** and **Ghosha**.

A well-known Rig Vedic thought says, in essence, that truth is one though the wise call it by many names — often seen as a root of Indian acceptance of many views.
keyTerms: Rishi — seer who composed hymns
Yajna — fire ritual
Rita — cosmic order

check.q: How were the Vedas preserved for many centuries?
options: Through precise oral memorisation and recitation
check.why: Teachers and students used careful recitation patterns to pass the Vedas on orally without change.

sections.md:
Later Vedic texts include the **Upanishads**. The word suggests 'sitting near' — students sitting near a teacher to learn deep truths. They are written as conversations and stories.

The Upanishads asked big questions: *Who am I? What is real? What happens after death? What is the source of everything?*

Two key ideas:

- **Brahman** — the ultimate reality, the one essence behind the whole universe.
- **Atman** — the inner self of each being. A central teaching is that the Atman and Brahman are, at the deepest level, one. A famous phrase, *tat tvam asi* ('that thou art'), expresses this.

This means every living being shares the same essence — a basis for treating all with respect.

The Upanishads are full of memorable stories. In one, a student called **Satyakama** honestly tells a teacher he does not know who his father is, and the teacher accepts him for his truthfulness. Women thinkers like **Gargi** and **Maitreyi** appear in debates — Gargi questions the sage Yajnavalkya so sharply in a royal assembly that he warns her not to push further! Ideas of **karma** (actions have consequences) and **rebirth** became widely discussed in this period.

check.q: In the Upanishads, what is the relationship taught between Atman and Brahman?
options: They are at the deepest level one
Atman is a god of fire
check.why: The Upanishads teach that the inner self (Atman) is ultimately one with the universal reality (Brahman).

sections.md:
Over centuries, Indian thinkers developed several systems of philosophy called **darshanas** ('ways of seeing'). Six are often listed together:

| School | Main focus |
|---|---|
| **Nyaya** | Logic and correct reasoning |
| **Vaisheshika** | Nature of matter; atoms (*paramanu*) |
| **Samkhya** | Matter (*prakriti*) and consciousness (*purusha*) |
| **Yoga** | Discipline of body and mind to reach inner freedom |
| **Mimamsa** | Interpreting Vedic ritual and duty |
| **Vedanta** | Interpreting the Upanishads |

There were other schools too, such as the **Charvaka** (or Lokayata), who doubted everything not seen by the senses. Thinkers debated openly; debating was itself a respected art, with rules about fair argument.

**Yoga** is perhaps the best-known gift to the world. The *Yoga Sutras* attributed to **Patanjali** describe an eight-limbed path, including ethical rules, postures (*asanas*), breath control (*pranayama*) and meditation. Since 2015, **21 June** is celebrated worldwide as **International Day of Yoga**.

check.q: Which school of philosophy focused mainly on logic and correct reasoning?
check.why: Nyaya developed careful rules of logic and debate for reaching correct knowledge.

sections.md:
Around the 6th–5th century BCE (scholars debate the exact dates), many new thinkers questioned ritual and searched for new answers. Among them was **Siddhartha Gautama**, a prince of the **Shakya** clan, born at **Lumbini** (in present-day Nepal).

Tradition says that on seeing an old man, a sick man, a dead body and a calm ascetic, he realised that all life involves suffering and change. He left his palace to seek the truth. After years of searching, he meditated under a **peepal tree** at **Bodh Gaya** (Bihar) and attained **enlightenment** — he became the **Buddha**, 'the awakened one'. That tree's descendant is called the **Bodhi tree**.

He gave his **first sermon** at **Sarnath** near Varanasi and taught for many years, travelling across north India. He passed away at **Kushinagar**.

**Core teachings**

- **Four Noble Truths**: life involves suffering (*dukkha*); suffering arises from craving; suffering can end; the way to end it is the Eightfold Path.
- **The Eightfold Path**: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
- **The Middle Path**: avoid both extreme luxury and extreme self-punishment.
- **Ahimsa** (non-violence) and **compassion** (*karuna*) for all beings.
- Everything changes — nothing is permanent.

He taught in **Pali/Prakrit**, the language of ordinary people, so everyone could understand. His followers formed the **sangha** (community of monks and nuns). Buddhism later spread across Asia — to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, China, Korea, Japan, Tibet — especially after Emperor Ashoka supported it.

keyTerms: Sangha — community of Buddhist monks and nuns
Dukkha — suffering
Middle Path — avoiding extremes

check.q: Where did the Buddha give his first sermon?
check.why: After enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, the Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath near Varanasi.

sections.md:
Jain tradition holds that its teachings were taught by a line of **24 Tirthankaras** ('ford-makers' who help people cross the river of rebirth). The 23rd was **Parshvanatha**, and the 24th was **Vardhamana Mahavira**, who lived around the same period as the Buddha.

Mahavira was born into a royal family near **Vaishali** (Bihar). At about 30, he left home, lived as an ascetic for about 12 years and attained **kevala jnana** (complete knowledge). He was called **Jina** ('conqueror' of the self) — and his followers are **Jains**.

**Key teachings**

- **Ahimsa** — total non-violence towards all living beings, even tiny insects. Some Jain monks sweep the path softly and cover their mouths to avoid harming creatures.
- **Satya** (truth), **asteya** (not stealing), **brahmacharya** (self-control), **aparigraha** (non-possession — not being attached to things).
- **Anekantavada** — the idea that reality has many sides and no single viewpoint holds the whole truth. The classic illustration is the story of blind men touching an elephant: one feels the trunk and says 'a snake', another the leg and says 'a pillar'. Each is partly right. This idea encourages listening to others' views.

Jain communities contributed greatly to Indian literature, mathematics, trade and art — like the Dilwara temples at Mount Abu and the huge statue of Bahubali (Gommateshwara) at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka.

check.q: The Jain idea that truth has many sides and no single view sees all of it is called:
check.why: Anekantavada, illustrated by the blind men and the elephant, teaches the many-sidedness of reality.

sections.md:
Not all roots are found in books. Alongside these texts, India's **folk** and **tribal** communities developed rich traditions passed down orally and through practice — songs, dances, stories, crafts and knowledge of forests, rivers and medicinal plants.

Some common features:

- **Nature is sacred.** Many communities worship hills, rivers, trees, animals and the Earth. Sacred groves — *devrai* in Maharashtra, *kavu* in Kerala, *orans* in Rajasthan, *sarna* among some communities in Jharkhand — are protected forest patches where no tree is cut.
- **Community and sharing.** Harvests and festivals are celebrated together.
- **Deep knowledge** of local ecology — which plant heals, when the rains come.

Examples: the **Bishnoi** community of Rajasthan is famous for protecting trees and blackbucks; the Warli painting tradition of Maharashtra; festivals like Sarhul in Jharkhand; Pithora painting among the Rathwa of Gujarat.

These traditions and the textual traditions influenced each other. Many deities, festivals and ideas moved between villages and scriptures. That two-way flow is why Indian culture became like the banyan — **many roots, one tree**.

check.q: What is a sacred grove?
options: A patch of forest protected by a community for religious reasons
check.why: Sacred groves are community-protected forests where cutting trees is forbidden, helping preserve biodiversity.

sections.h: Shared values: the trunk of the banyan
sections.md:
Look across all these roots and you find ideas that keep returning, even though the traditions differ in many ways:

| Value | Where we meet it |
|---|---|
| **Dharma** — right conduct, duty | From Vedic *rita* to Buddhist and Jain teaching |
| **Ahimsa** — non-violence | Upanishads, Buddha, Mahavira; later Gandhi |
| **Karma** — actions have results | Upanishads, Buddhism, Jainism |
| **Respect for nature** | Vedic hymns, sacred groves, Bishnoi practice |
| **Questioning and debate** | Nasadiya Sukta, Upanishadic dialogues, darshanas |
| **Accepting many views** | 'Truth is one, called by many names'; anekantavada |
| **Seva and sharing** | Community feasts, care for guests and the needy |

These shared values helped very different communities live side by side and learn from one another. They also travelled far: Buddhism shaped cultures across Asia; yoga and meditation are practised worldwide; **Mahatma Gandhi** drew on ahimsa for India's freedom struggle; and the **Chipko** movement in the Himalayas, where villagers hugged trees to save them, echoed the Bishnoi spirit.

> Think about it: Which of these values do you see in your own family, school or neighbourhood? Which would you most like to practise more?

check.q: Which value appears in the Upanishads, Buddhism and Jainism and later inspired Gandhi?
check.why: Ahimsa, non-violence, is central to all three traditions and became the heart of Gandhi's struggle.

story.title: Nachiketa at the Door of Death (a retelling from the Katha Upanishad)

parts.md:
Long ago, a man named Vajashravas held a great ritual and gave away gifts — but only his old, useless cows. His young son **Nachiketa** felt this was not true giving. "Father, to whom will you give me?" he asked. He asked again, and again. Annoyed, his father snapped, "To Death I give you!"

Nachiketa took the words seriously. He went to the house of **Yama**, the lord of death. Yama was away, and the boy waited at the door for three days and nights without food or water.

When Yama returned, he was ashamed that a guest had waited so long. "Choose three boons," he said. Nachiketa asked first that his father be calm and welcome him home; second, to learn a sacred fire ritual. Both were granted at once.

For the third, Nachiketa asked: "What happens to a person after death? Tell me the truth of the self." Yama hesitated. "Ask for anything else — long life, cattle, gold, kingdoms, music and dancing!" But Nachiketa replied that all such things fade. "Keep your riches. I want to know the truth."

Pleased by the boy's steadiness, Yama taught him that the true self, the Atman, is not born and does not die; it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. He explained that wise people choose the *good* (shreyas) over the merely *pleasant* (preyas).

Nachiketa returned home with knowledge greater than any treasure. The story is still told to show that a sincere question, asked with courage, is worth more than riches.

summary: Indian culture is like a banyan tree — many roots and branches forming one whole.
There are four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva; the Rig Veda is the oldest.
The Vedas were preserved orally with great precision; Vedic chanting is UNESCO-recognised heritage.
Vedic ideas include rita (cosmic order), respect for nature, open questioning and assemblies (sabha, samiti).
The Upanishads explore Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (self), teaching their oneness; Gargi and Maitreyi took part in debates.
Six classical darshanas: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta; Charvaka was a sceptical school.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras; 21 June is International Day of Yoga.
The Buddha: born Lumbini, enlightened at Bodh Gaya, first sermon at Sarnath, died at Kushinagar.
Buddhism teaches the Four Noble Truths, Eightfold Path and Middle Path; it spread across Asia.
Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara; Jainism stresses ahimsa, five vows and anekantavada.
Folk and tribal traditions treat nature as sacred and protect sacred groves.
Shared values — dharma, ahimsa, karma, respect for nature, debate, many views, seva — link all the roots.

glossary.d: A system of philosophy; 'way of seeing'.
In Jainism, a teacher who shows the way across the cycle of rebirth.
Non-violence.
Buddhist monastic community.
Philosophical texts; literally 'sitting near' a teacher.

rd-school-c6-social-b.ch08-unity-diversi.title: Unity in Diversity, or 'Many in the One'
rd-school-c6-social-b.ch08-unity-diversi.subtitle: Rice and roti, saris and stories, a hundred festivals — and the threads that tie them into one fabric

sections.md:
Board the **Vivek Express**, one of India's longest train routes, at Dibrugarh in Assam and get off at Kanniyakumari, about 4,200 km and roughly three days later. On the way, your food changes: fish curry and rice in Assam, *machher jhol* in Bengal, *dalma* in Odisha, spicy *pulihora* in Andhra, and finally *sambar*, *rasam* and coconut chutney in Tamil Nadu. Announcements at stations switch from Assamese to Bengali, Odia, Telugu, Tamil. Clothes, scripts on signboards and temple shapes change too.

Yet everyone on the train calls themselves Indian. Fellow passengers share snacks, children play together, and the same cricket score excites the whole coach.

This is what we mean by **unity in diversity** — or as the chapter title puts it, **'many in the one'**. India's diversity is like the many colours of a rainbow, which together make one arc of light.

In this chapter we explore:

- the **diversity** of India's land, languages, food, clothing and festivals;
- the **unity** that runs beneath — shared values, stories, ideas, arts and history;
- how diversity and unity are not opposites but **strengthen each other**.

India is vast — over 32 lakh square kilometres — with snowy mountains, deserts, plains, plateaus, forests, coasts and islands. Different landscapes and climates have led people to develop different ways of living: stone houses with sloping roofs in Himachal, bamboo homes on stilts in Assam, thick-walled mud houses in Rajasthan, airy tiled houses in Kerala.

India also has many **communities**: people of different regions, languages, religions and tribes. Our Constitution recognises 22 languages in its **Eighth Schedule**, and censuses have recorded well over a thousand mother tongues. Followers of Hinduism, Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism (Parsis), Judaism and tribal faiths live together.

This diversity is not new. For thousands of years, people moved within the subcontinent and others came from outside — traders, travellers, refugees, scholars. Ideas, crafts and words travelled with them and blended into Indian life.

check.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution?
check.why: The Eighth Schedule currently lists 22 scheduled languages.

sections.h: Unity in language: words and scripts that travel
sections.md:
With so many languages, how do Indians understand each other? There are deeper links than you might think.

- **Shared word-stock.** Words travel freely between Indian languages. *Kamal* (lotus), *nagar* (town), *jal* (water) appear in many northern and southern languages; Tamil words like *kattumaram* gave English 'catamaran', and Malayalam *inchi* is linked to 'ginger'. Persian and Arabic gave Hindi, Urdu, Marathi, Bengali and others words like *kitab*, *darwaza*, *zameen*.
- **Related scripts.** Most Indian scripts — Devanagari, Bengali, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and even Sinhala, Thai and Tibetan — descend from the ancient **Brahmi** script of Ashoka's time. That is why their alphabets follow the same order: vowels first, then consonants grouped by where in the mouth they are spoken (*ka, kha, ga…*).
- **Bilingual living.** Most Indians speak two or three languages — a Kannada-speaking child in Bengaluru may use Hindi with a friend, English in class and Tamil with a neighbour.

So India's languages are less like separate islands and more like a family of rivers that keep meeting.

check.q: Most Indian scripts descend from which ancient script?
check.why: Brahmi, used in Ashoka's inscriptions, is the ancestor of most scripts of South and Southeast Asia.

sections.md:
Indian food varies wildly — but look closer and you find shared patterns:

- **Staple + accompaniment.** Almost everywhere, a meal has a staple (rice, wheat roti, millet bhakri, ragi mudde) with dal or a vegetable or fish curry.
- **Spices** like turmeric, cumin, coriander, ginger and black pepper are used across regions, though in different combinations. Black pepper from Kerala was once so precious it was called 'black gold' in world trade.
- **The thali** — a plate with small bowls of many dishes — exists in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and beyond. In the south, the same idea is served on a banana leaf.
- **Ideas about food**: food is often seen as sacred (*prasad*), meant to be shared (langar in gurudwaras feeds anyone who comes), and balanced for health — many traditions speak of six tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent.
- **Millets** — jowar, bajra, ragi — were eaten across India for millennia. The United Nations declared **2023 the International Year of Millets**, an idea proposed by India.

So the dishes differ, but the *grammar* of the meal is shared.

check.q: Which idea about food is shared across many Indian regions?
options: A staple served with several accompaniments
check.why: Whether rice, roti or ragi, most Indian meals pair a staple with dal, vegetables or curry — the thali pattern.

sections.h: Unity in clothing: the story of the sari
sections.md:
Clothing in India changes with climate and community: woollen *pherans* in Kashmir, *mekhela chador* in Assam, *mundu* and *veshti* in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, *ghagra-choli* in Rajasthan, *kurta-pyjama*, *salwar-kameez*, the *dhoti*, the turban tied in dozens of regional styles.

The **sari** is a wonderful example of many-in-one. It is basically an **unstitched length of cloth**, usually 5 to 9 yards (about 4.5 to 8 m), worn across much of India. Yet:

- it is **draped in over a hundred ways** — the Nivi style, the Bengali style with pleats and a key-bunch on the pallu, the Maharashtrian *nauvari* tucked like a dhoti, the Coorgi style with pleats at the back, the Gujarati style with the pallu in front;
- it is **woven differently** in each region: Banarasi silk (Uttar Pradesh), Kanjeevaram (Tamil Nadu), Paithani (Maharashtra), Patola (Gujarat), Baluchari (West Bengal), Sambalpuri and Bomkai (Odisha), Muga silk (Assam), Pochampally ikat (Telangana), Chanderi (Madhya Pradesh).

Ancient sculptures and texts show draped unstitched garments going back thousands of years. India's **handloom** heritage is so important that **7 August** is observed as **National Handloom Day**, recalling the Swadeshi movement launched on 7 August 1905.

head: Sari style
Region
fig.caption: One garment, many weaves.

check.q: Why is the sari a good example of 'many in the one'?
options: It is worn only in one state
It is one basic garment draped and woven in many regional ways
It is always made of the same cloth
check.why: The sari is a single unstitched garment found across India, yet each region has its own weave and drape.

sections.md:
India celebrates hundreds of festivals. Many share **themes** even when names differ:

**Harvest festivals** mark the gathering of crops, usually in mid-January when the Sun enters Makara (Capricorn), and again in spring or autumn:

| Festival | Region |
|---|---|
| Makar Sankranti | Many states |
| Pongal | Tamil Nadu |
| Lohri | Punjab |
| Magh Bihu / Bhogali Bihu | Assam |
| Uttarayan (kite festival) | Gujarat |
| Onam | Kerala (harvest in Aug–Sept) |
| Baisakhi | Punjab (spring harvest) |
| Nuakhai | Odisha |

**New Year festivals** in spring: Ugadi (Karnataka, Andhra, Telangana), Gudi Padwa (Maharashtra), Puthandu (Tamil Nadu), Vishu (Kerala), Bohag Bihu (Assam), Pohela Boishakh (Bengal), Baisakhi (Punjab), Navreh (Kashmir) — all around March–April.

**Festivals of light** — Diwali, Kartik Purnima, Dev Deepawali; and festivals like Christmas and Guru Nanak Jayanti are celebrated with lights too.

Indians also share in each other's festivals: neighbours exchange sweets at Eid, Diwali and Christmas; everyone flies kites at Uttarayan; people of all communities visit Durga Puja pandals.

The common threads: gratitude to nature, the turning of seasons, sharing food, family gatherings and new beginnings.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 340' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='340' fill='#1a237e'/><g fill='#ffeb3b'><circle cx='60' cy='40' r='2'/><circle cx='520' cy='60' r='2'/><circle cx='300' cy='30' r='2'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;10 -15;0 0' dur='4s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><polygon points='140,70 175,110 140,150 105,110' fill='#e91e63'/><path d='M140 150 Q 150 200 130 260' stroke='#fff' fill='none'/></g><g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-12 -10;0 0' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/><polygon points='460,60 490,95 460,130 430,95' fill='#00bcd4'/><path d='M460 130 Q 450 190 470 260' stroke='#fff' fill='none'/></g><g transform='translate(300 270)'><path d='M-40 20 Q0 50 40 20 Q0 30 -40 20Z' fill='#ff8f00'/><ellipse cx='0' cy='5' rx='7' ry='14' fill='#ffca28'><animate attributeName='ry' values='12;18;12' dur='0.7s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></ellipse></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#fff' text-anchor='middle'><text x='300' y='140'>Kites of Uttarayan, diyas of Diwali,</text><text x='300' y='162'>bonfires of Lohri and Bihu —</text><text x='300' y='184'>one gratitude, many forms</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Different festivals, shared joy.
fig.alt: Two kites gently floating in a night sky above a flickering diya.

check.q: Pongal, Lohri, Bihu and Makar Sankranti share which common theme?
check.why: All are celebrated around mid-January to thank nature for the harvest as the Sun moves northward.

sections.h: Unity in music, dance and art
sections.md:
India's arts also show many forms built on shared foundations.

- **Music.** Hindustani music in the north and Carnatic music in the south sound different, yet both rest on the same ideas of **raga** (melodic framework) and **tala** (rhythmic cycle), with roots traced to old texts like the *Natyashastra*. Folk songs — Baul songs of Bengal, Lavani of Maharashtra, Bihu songs of Assam — sing of love, harvest and the divine in local tongues.
- **Dance.** Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (north India), Kathakali and Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur) and Sattriya (Assam) are recognised classical dances. Each has its own costume and style, but all use **mudras** (hand gestures) and **abhinaya** (expression) to tell stories, often from the epics.
- **Art and craft.** Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Kalamkari (Andhra Pradesh) — different styles, shared love of nature, gods and village life. **Rangoli**, *kolam*, *alpana* and *mandana* are floor designs made at doorsteps across India under different names.

> Did you know? The *kolam* drawn with rice flour at Tamil doorsteps each morning also feeds ants and birds — an artwork that is also an act of sharing.

check.q: What do Bharatanatyam, Kathak and Odissi have in common?
options: They are all from one state
They use mudras and expressions to tell stories
check.why: All classical dances share a common grammar of hand gestures and expression, though each has its own style.

sections.h: Unity in stories, ideas and history
sections.md:
**Shared stories.** The **Ramayana** and **Mahabharata** are told in nearly every Indian language and art form, each with local flavour: Kamban's Tamil Ramayana, Krittivas's Bengali Ramayana, Tulsidas's *Ramcharitmanas* in Awadhi, Ezhuthachan's Malayalam version, and many folk, tribal and Southeast Asian versions — Ramlila, Kathakali, Yakshagana, shadow puppetry. The **Panchatantra** fables travelled from India to Persia, Arabia and Europe over centuries.

**Shared sacred geography.** Pilgrims have long criss-crossed the land: to the four *dhams* (Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram), the *jyotirlingas*, the *shakti peethas*, Buddhist sites like Bodh Gaya, Sikh gurudwaras like Hemkund Sahib and the Golden Temple, Sufi shrines like Ajmer Sharif, churches like Bom Jesus in Goa. A pilgrim from Kerala at a shrine in the Himalayas experiences the land as one.

**Shared values.** Respect for elders, hospitality (*atithi devo bhava*, 'the guest is like a god'), care for nature, non-violence, and the idea of the world as one family — *vasudhaiva kutumbakam* (a phrase from the Maha Upanishad) — are widely shared.

**Shared history and Constitution.** People from every region fought together in the freedom struggle. Our **Constitution** protects everyone's right to their language, religion and culture while making all citizens equal. The national anthem names regions from Punjab to Banga and from the Vindhyas and Himalayas to the seas.

> Did you know? The Indian rupee note carries its value in 15 languages on its language panel, besides Hindi and English on the front.

check.q: Vasudhaiva kutumbakam means:
check.why: The phrase from the Maha Upanishad means the whole world is one family.

sections.md:
Some people imagine that unity means everyone should be the same. India shows another way: **unity does not require uniformity**.

- Diversity brings **creativity** — music, food, crafts and ideas enrich one another (think of how Hindustani and Carnatic music, or Mughlai and regional cuisines, developed).
- It teaches **tolerance and respect** — learning to live with differences.
- It gives **resilience** — many ways of solving problems (dozens of water-harvesting traditions, many farming systems).

Of course, diversity can also bring misunderstanding or conflict when people stereotype each other. That is why learning about each other matters. Next time you meet a classmate from another state, ask about their festival, their food, their language — and share yours.

**Many in the one, and the one in the many** — that is the Indian way.

check.q: Which statement best captures 'unity in diversity'?
options: People with different cultures share common bonds and values
check.why: Unity in diversity means people keep their own cultures while sharing common bonds, values and identity.

parts.md: On the first day at a new school in Pune, Class 6B had students from seven states. The class teacher, Mrs Fernandes, announced a 'tiffin exchange' every Friday. Anirban brought luchi and aloo; Lalremsiami from Mizoram brought sticky rice with a little bamboo-shoot chutney; Harpreet brought aloo paratha; Meenakshi brought lemon rice; Zoya brought sheer khurma left over from Eid; Rohan brought poha with peanuts.

By December the class had a list on the wall: 'Our 32 Festivals'. They had flown kites for Sankranti with Rohan's family, eaten plum cake with Mrs Fernandes at Christmas, and learnt to say 'thank you' in nine languages.

At the annual day, 6B performed a song in which each child sang one line in their mother tongue and everyone sang the chorus together in Hindi and English. The audience could not understand every line — but they understood the whole song.

summary: India is diverse in land, climate, languages, religions, food, clothing and festivals.
The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages; India has hundreds of mother tongues.
Words travel between languages, and most Indian scripts descend from Brahmi.
Food differs but shares patterns: staple plus dishes, common spices, the thali, food as sacred and shared.
2023 was the International Year of Millets.
The sari is one unstitched garment with many regional weaves and drapes.
National Handloom Day is 7 August, recalling the Swadeshi movement of 1905.
Harvest festivals (Pongal, Lohri, Bihu, Sankranti, Onam) and spring New Years show shared themes.
Classical music rests on raga and tala; classical dances share mudras and abhinaya; folk arts share themes.
The Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra are retold across languages and art forms.
Pilgrimage routes connect all corners of India into a shared sacred geography.
Shared values: hospitality, respect for nature, non-violence, vasudhaiva kutumbakam.
The Constitution protects cultural rights and equal citizenship.
Unity does not mean uniformity; diversity is a source of strength and creativity.

glossary.d: Variety and difference.
Everything being the same.
Cloth woven by hand on a loom.
Melodic framework in Indian music.
The world is one family.
